**Peripherals (Bordure or Orle)** row — used for Peripheral Ordinaries (Table B.1 results 10–12). The six options are Bordure, Orle, Chief, Quarter/Canton and two further Chief placements. *(Column-order note: this row was reconstructed from a column-jumbled PDF extract; re-verify the exact 1D6 slot ordering against p.246 before relying on it.)*

## Blazoning (writing the arms down)

A coat of arms is described in words ("blazoning") so it can be reconstructed exactly. Blazon from the "bottom" up: first the **Field** and all its divisions/furs/patterns, then the **Ordinaries** (and any charges on them), then the **Subordinaries** (and their charges), then any other **Charges**.

### Worked examples

- **Sir Lycus, Bachelor Knight** — Shield 1D20=12 (Peripheral Ordinary + Charge on the Ordinary); Field 1D20=17 → Vert; Ordinary tincture Metal 1D20=1 → Argent; Charge tincture Color 1D20=15 → Sable; Peripherals 1D6=3 → a Chief; Charge col.1 row 16 → a Wolf (1D3=1, 1D6=3 full animal). **Blazon: *Vert, on a chief argent a sable wolf.***
- **Sir Iowerth of Eastridge** — Shield 1D20=14 (Ordinary + Charge on the Field); Field 1D20=10 → Purpure; Ordinary Metal 1D20=6 → Argent; Charge Metal 1D20=1 → Argent; Ordinary col.6 1D6=4 → a Bend; Charge col.5 row 12 → a Mullet of 6/8 (1D2=2 → 8 points; 1D3=2 → two stars). **Blazon: *Purpure, a bend between two mullets of eight argent.***

title: Horse Colors, Personality, Care & Armor (Tables 10.5–10.7)
text:
## Colors & Passive Glory

A horse's color is a social identifier and grants **Passive Glory** (once per year per color owned; different colors stack):

- **White** — 50 (born white, rare; a grand gift only, not purchasable).
- **Gray** — 25 (+£25) · **Bay** — 15 (+£15) · **Yellow** — 5 (+£5; the minimum acceptable steed for a Superlative-standard knight/lady).
- **Pale** — hard to find (fairy/omen horses); **Black** — least expensive.

## Table 10.5 — Horse Personality (roll 1D3 times; no mechanical effect)

1 Loyal · 2 Willing · 3 Gentle · 4 Affectionate · 5 Steady · 6 Alert · 7 Resilient · 8 Careful · 9 Fairy-touched · 10 Intelligent · 11 Aggressive · 12 Brave · 13 Opinionated · 14 Mischievous · 15 Chowhound · 16 Nervous · 17 Biter · 18 Destructive · 19 Clumsy · 20 Challenging. A foal inherits each parent trait on a **1–3 on 1D6**.

## Care & First Aid — Table 10.6

If a horse endures something extraordinary, takes damage, or is wounded, roll **Horsemanship**:

| Result | Immediate | Long-term |
|--------|-----------|-----------|
| Critical | Energized: may move fast for **double** the normal duration | No effect |
| Success | Carries on as normal | No effect |
| Failure | Weak/sore: **−5** to all Horsemanship rolls until a farrier tends it | **−1** to next Winter Phase Horse Survival Roll |
| Fumble | Terribly weak/sore: **−10** until a farrier tends it | **−2** to next Horse Survival Roll |

A character with **Horsemanship 15+** may apply **First Aid** to wounded steeds: horse Healing Rate = CON/5, one roll per wound (as for humans).

## Table 10.7 — Horse Armor

| Type | Armor | Horse STR needed | Notes |
|------|-------|------------------|-------|
| Caparison, Open | 0 | Any | decorative |
| Caparison, Half | 0 | Any | decorative |
| Caparison, Full | 0 | Any | weather protection, decorative |
| Padding, Full | 1 | 30 | Small Charger and greater |
| Gambeson, Half | 2 | 32 | Charger and greater |
| Gambeson, Full | 4 | 34 | Large Charger and greater |

Horse armor is **not** issued automatically (even to household knights); horses must have sufficient **STR** to wear it.

title: Horses Taking Damage — Wounds, Knockdown, Crushing & Recovery
text:
Horses are damaged like characters — their own `SIZ`/`CON`/Hit Points, wounds recorded normally. Three things are specific to them: a **5-point threshold** that degrades the rider's control, the **horse's `SIZ`** as the knockdown trigger for *both* animal and rider, and the fact that **only a character with `Horsemanship 15+`** may treat one.

## Getting the horse hit

- **Attacking a horse deliberately** is dishonorable between knights: **−1 Honor**. A **partial success** by the rider lets the horse benefit from his **Shield/Parry Protection**. Attacking from foot negates the attacker's −5 Height penalty, but the mounted opponent still gets their **+5**. *(ch. 7, pp. 137–138)*
- **Missiles** do not discriminate: each round of barrage, roll **1D6 — 1–4 hits the mount, 5–6 the rider**. *(GM Book, ch. 6 — Battle, pp. 129–130)*
- **Horse armor** is **not issued automatically**, even to household knights, and the horse needs the **STR** to wear it. *(Table 10.7, p. 187)*

| Type | Armor | Horse STR needed |
|---|---:|---|
| Caparison (open / half / full) | 0 | Any — decorative |
| Padding, Full | 1 | 30 (Small Charger and greater) |
| Gambeson, Half | 2 | 32 (Charger and greater) |
| Gambeson, Full | 4 | 34 (Large Charger and greater) |

## The 5-point threshold

**When any horse takes 5+ points of damage in a round**, check injury effects — and thereafter **roll `Horsemanship` every round before acting, at a penalty equal to the horse's total lost Hit Points**. A combat-trained horse settles on a critical *or* an ordinary success. *(CRB, pp. 181)*  A failed role means the horse will not settle and the entire round is spent trying to get the horse under control.  Once settled a horse won't need another check unless wounded again.

The injury check is **Table 10.6**, rolled on `Horsemanship` *(p. 187)* if the GM feels the horse needs immediate and extra care (crb187):

| Result | Immediate | Long-term |
|---|---|---|
| **Critical** | Energized — may move fast for **double** the normal duration | No effect |
| **Success** | Carries on as normal | No effect |
| **Failure** | Weak/sore: **−5** to all `Horsemanship` rolls until a farrier tends it | **−1** to the next Winter Phase Horse Survival Roll |
| **Fumble** | Terribly weak/sore: **−10** until a farrier tends it | **−2** to that roll |

## Going down — the horse's SIZ is the trigger

**If total damage to *either* horse or rider exceeds the horse's `SIZ`**, the **horse** makes a `DEX` roll to stay standing; failure knocks it down. *(ch. 7, p. 150; and p. 134)*

The rider then attempts an **Emergency Dismount** — unopposed `Horsemanship`, **Table 7.4**:

- **Critical:** lands on his feet, upright next round, no damage, **keeps all weapons**.
- **Success:** lands on his feet, no damage, but **drops** held weapons.
- **Failure:** improper dismount — **1D6** damage, drops all weapons.
- **Fumble:** **2D6** damage, drops all weapons; **if the horse fell, it lands on him for the horse's Damage**.

If the Emergency Dismount fails outright the rider is **crushed by the falling steed for the horse's normal Damage** — armor protects normally. *(ch. 7, pp. 150–151)*

**Escaping from under a fallen horse:** each round, roll the rider's **`STR` vs the horse's `SIZ`**; each helper adds **+5** to the strongest person's `STR`, who makes the roll.

> Distinguish this from an ordinary fall from the saddle, which is only **1D6**.

## Treating and replacing it

- ==**Only a character with `Horsemanship 15+` may apply `First Aid` to a wounded steed.**== Horse **Healing Rate = CON/5**, one roll per wound, as for humans. *(p. 187)*
- **In battle:** a successful **`Squire` roll** brings a fresh horse mid-fight, and **Retiring to the Rear** allows lost horses to be replaced on **`Squire Skill` or `Horsemanship`**. ==Being unhorsed **and** failing the Squire roll for a remount leaves the knight **Alone on the Field**== — his own commander at **Battle −10**, still draining the conroi's Morale. *(GM Book, ch. 6, pp. 130–132)*
- **At year's end:** every charger, destrier, or unique horse rolls **1D20 on Table 14.7, the Horse Survival Roll** — where a failed or fumbled Table 10.6 check returns as a **−1 or −2**. *(ch. 14, p. 232)*

## Adjacent rules that bite in the same moment

- **Mounted Charge fumble** with a couched lance sends the rider to **Table 7.2**: a failure buries the tip and launches him from the saddle for **2D6**; a fumble brings **both him and the horse** down for **3D6**. Armor protects against neither. *(p. 141)*
- **Trample** works only on **prone** opponents and uses the horse's **normal (non-charging) Damage**. *(pp. 142–143)*
- **Too Big for Your Horse** — if the rider's `SIZ`×2 (−5 if unarmored) exceeds the horse's `STR`: **−5** `Horsemanship`, **−5** horse Movement Rate, counts as Forced March on long travel, and horse Damage **−1D6**. *(ch. 7, p. 151)*

title: Horse Speeds, Exhaustion (Table 10.1) & Training
text:
## Gaits

- **Walk** — slowest; sets the Movement Rate.
- **Trot** — Move ×2 · **Canter** — Move ×3 · **Gallop** — Move ×6.

Any gait holds for a scene, but **galloping over 15 minutes risks the horse's health**. **Ambling** is a special smooth gait (same pace as a trot, far less tiring) only certain individual horses have; they cost much more.

## Riding to death (overuse)

Overuse comes from galloping >15 min, riding day and night, no rest, a forced march, or poor food/water. At the end of the abuse, roll the horse's **CON** and consult Table 10.1.

### Table 10.1 — Horse Exhaustion Roll

| Horse CON roll | Effect |
|----------------|--------|
| Critical | No problem |
| Success | Too tired to continue; recovers with food and rest |
| Failure | **Blown** — cannot canter/gallop and never fully recovers |
| Fumble | Horse **drops dead** |

## Training

Light training at **age 3**, proper training at **4**: ~**1 year** for basic riding, **2 years** to be trusted for mounted combat. War horses peak around **8**, decline after ~**15**, and retire from heavy work by **20**. Best trained by being ridden by a skilled knight through many experiences.

**Breeding** determines potential — destriers come only from destriers, amblers from amblers (with some fluidity: a great courser might make a decent charger). All horses know the simple trick of **standing in place** when the rider dismounts or is unhorsed. **Unique tricks** (come when called, rear, dance, count, etc.) cost **+25% (one), +50% (two), +75% (three features)**.

title: Horse Types & Stats (Tables 10.2–10.4)
text:
**Normal Damage** = trampling/hooves; **Charge Damage** = a spear/lance rider's successful Mounted Charge; **Move** = walking Movement Rate.

## Table 10.2 — Combat Horses

| Type | Normal | Charge | Move | Armor | SIZ | DEX | STR | CON | HP | Comments |
|------|--------|--------|------|-------|-----|-----|-----|-----|----|----|
| Charger, small | 3D6 | 5D6 | 15 | 4 | 32 | 13 | 30 | 12 | 44 | may wear padding/half gambeson |

title: Aggravation (Table 11.2) & Deterioration
text:
## Aggravation — worsening a condition through activity

Making a condition worse through activity while ill or injured.

**Effect: 1 or more points of damage subtracted from current Hit Points, with no wound recorded.** **One point is the normal loss**; a character may suffer **up to 3** from extremely violent or sustained activity (the book's example is mortal combat with an ogre) at the GM's option. **First Aid cannot cure or reduce Aggravation damage.**

Aggravation damage occurs **after the activity is complete**, unless the GM decides otherwise — so a character may **lose consciousness immediately after the rash action** that earned it.

Applied by incident (GM judgment), not weekly; current health, the extent of injuries, and the duration and intensity of the activity all matter. Aggravation is possible for **any injured character, Healthy or Debilitated**, undertaking **strenuous** activity; **Debilitated characters may suffer it on even moderate activity**. Characters **below the Unconscious level cannot take Aggravation** — they can perform only light activity and are normally comatose. **Chirurgery cannot halt Aggravation.**

For the per-round case — fighting on past Unconscious or after a Major Wound, which costs **1 Aggravation per round** — see [[core.injury-health.states-of-health-and-wounds]].

### Table 11.2 — Activity and Aggravation

| Activity | Examples | Healthy | Debilitated |
|----------|----------|---------|-------------|
| **No activity** | rest, eat sensibly, sleep | None (best recovery) | None (best recovery) |
| **Light** | short walks, conversation, short letters | None | None unless overdone |
| **Moderate** | longer walks, riding (even briefly), dancing, romance, arguing | None | Possible (GM option) |
| **Strenuous** | fighting, running, climbing, significant travel | Possible if many small wounds or below half HP | **Certain** |

## Deterioration — untended wounds worsening

**1D6 damage per week** to **Debilitated** characters who do **not** get a successful Chirurgery roll that week (no wound recorded; First Aid can't help). It occurs **immediately before** the weekly natural Healing Rate is applied. Only one Chirurgery roll is allowed per week (Deterioration hits on a failure/fumble).

title: Environmental Damage — Cold, Falling, Fire, Suffocation & Poison (Table 11.3)
text:
## Cold

Unopposed **CON roll**; **failure/fumble = 1D6** taken directly from HP (no wound). Roll **once per day** in cold, **every round** in freezing (e.g. fording an ice-choked river). Chirurgery restores **half** the cold points (**all** on a critical).

## Disease

Rare (usually from a deep dungeon). GM sets the damage (usually Characteristic/HP loss, no wound). A diseased character is **Debilitated**.

## Falling

<2 yards = no damage. **2 yards = 1D6**, +1D6 per additional 2 yards, **max 16D6**. **Armor does not absorb** falling damage. A **Horsemanship** roll (falling from a horse) or **DEX** roll (otherwise) **removes 1D6** dice (2D6 on a critical); a **fumble doubles** the dice. Record as one wound.

## Falling objects

Small (palm-sized rock) **2D6**; boulders/masonry **3D6+**, up to **16D6**. **Armor protects normally**; an aware character may add **Shield** Protection (not Parry). Each is a separate wound.

## Fire & Heat

**1D6 per Combat Round.** Armor protects for **only one round**, then is too hot until a one-round break to cool. Great heat (wyrm's breath) may do **2D6+** or ignore armor. All fire damage is a **single wound**; one First Aid roll per instance.

## Suffocation (water, smoke, vapors)

Unopposed **CON roll each round** (holding breath); once failed, **1D6/round** while exposed (more if toxic). A **cumulative −1 to CON per round** beyond the first (7th round = −6). No wounds; recovery from near-drowning may be rapid (GM option).

## Poison

Every poison has a **Potency**. On introduction, make an **opposed CON roll vs the fixed Potency** (Fixed Opposition).

### Table 11.3 — Poisoning Results

| CON result | Effect |
|------------|--------|
| Win | No effect |
| Partial success | Lose **half** the Potency from CON |
| Loss | Lose the **full** Potency from CON |

**Sample potencies:** Foxglove 5 · Dwale (Belladonna) 10 · Hemlock 15 · Arsenic 20 · Wolfsbane/Monkshood 25. **CON 0 = death** (recompute derived stats as CON drops). Lost CON returns at the **Healing Rate per week**.

**Antidotes:** a successful **Chirurgery** roll provides one (ingested then vomited), before CON hits 0. Unicorn horn, emerald powder, bezoars, and toadstones are believed to cancel poison; a **taster** is the surest prevention.

title: Falling from a Horse — Emergency Dismount, Horsemanship vs DEX
text:
If you are unseated, thrown, or falling from a horse, the primary roll you make to minimize or avoid damage is an **unopposed Horsemanship roll**. However, depending on the exact circumstances of your fall, the rules also call for an **unopposed DEX roll** in certain situations.

Here is how both rolls work to keep your knight safe:

### **1. The Horsemanship Roll (The Standard Fall)**

When you are about to fall, be thrown from your mount, or if your horse slips or falls due to wounds, you attempt an **Emergency Dismount** using your **Horsemanship skill**. The outcomes are resolved as follows:

- **Critical Success:** You land gracefully on your feet and begin the next round upright (if conscious). You take **no damage** from the fall and retain all of your weapons.
- **Normal Success:** You land on your feet upright and ready to act next round. You take **no damage** from the fall, but you drop any weapons you were holding.
- **Failure:** You fail to dismount properly. You take **1D6 falling damage** and drop all held weapons.
- **Fumble:** You take **2D6 falling damage** and drop your weapons. Additionally, if your horse fell as well, it lands directly on top of you, inflicting its full normal Damage value (though your armor protects against the horse's weight normally).

Alternatively, if you are falling from a horse in a more general sense, a successful Horsemanship roll simply **reduces the falling damage dice by 1D6** (or by **2D6 on a critical success**). Be careful, though: a fumble on this roll **doubles** the number of damage dice you take!

---

### **2. The DEX Roll (Unconsciousness and General Fall-Breaking)**

There are specific exceptions where the rules direct you to use your **DEX characteristic** instead of Horsemanship to survive a fall:

- **Falling Unconscious:** If you suffer a Major Wound or your Hit Points drop below your Unconscious threshold while mounted, you will begin to slide off your horse. In this life-or-death moment, you attempt an Emergency Dismount using an **unopposed DEX roll**. A success means you fall gently and take **no damage**; a failure means you suffer a bad fall for **1D6 damage**.
- **Breaking a Fall:** The Gamemaster’s Handbook notes that the hazard of being thrown or knocked from a horse, or falling from a height, can be offset with a **DEX roll**.
- **Other Falls:** If you are falling from anything _other_ than a horse (like a castle wall or a steep slope), a **DEX roll** is used instead of Horsemanship to reduce the damage dice.

🛡️ If you do find yourself on the ground, your squire can be a lifesaver—would you like to see how a Squire Roll is used in battle to get you a fresh mount or pull you out of danger?

title: Healing & Recovery — Natural Healing, Chirurgery & First Aid
text:
Characters heal only through **natural healing**, **Chirurgery**, **First Aid**, or magic/miracle. Weekly healing conventionally occurs **Sunday at noon**; insisting on activity instead of rest triggers **Aggravation**.

## Natural Healing

Restores **Healing Rate** (= CON/5) HP per week. Deterioration and Aggravation may make a week's net result nil or a loss.

## Chirurgery (for Debilitated characters — halts Deterioration)

One roll per week (Sunday noon). **−5** in unclean/unhealthy conditions.

- **Critical:** no Deterioration, **and** add the Healing Rate to current HP now.
- **Success:** no Deterioration.
- **Failure:** Deterioration occurs.
- **Fumble:** Deterioration occurs **and** lose 1D6 HP.

## First Aid (emergency, per wound, fresh wounds < 1 day)

Each wound takes ≥ 5 minutes (not during combat). A **failed** attempt bars any further First Aid on that wound. First Aid on Major/Mortal wounds does **not** clear the Debilitated state. May be attempted **on oneself at −10**; a squire may attempt it if no PKs are present.

- **Critical:** regain **double Healing Rate** (up to the wound's value).
- **Success:** regain **Healing Rate** (up to the wound's value).
- **Failure:** no improvement.
- **Fumble:** lose **1D3 HP** directly and become **Debilitated**.

title: States of Health & Wounds (Minor/Major/Mortal, Unconscious, Near Death)
text:
A character is either **Healthy** or **Debilitated** (no middle ground). Healthy characters need no care and heal weekly at their Healing Rate, even below full HP.

**The Debilitated box is checked when a character:** drops below the Unconscious Characteristic; takes a Major Wound; survives a Mortal Wound; fumbles a First Aid roll; or contracts illness/poison. It stays checked until a **successful Chirurgery roll** and recovery to **half Total HP**.

## Wounds

Each hit is a separate **wound** = damage dealt minus Armor (and Shield/Parry) Protection; record each separately (First Aid is per-wound). Three types by the size of a **single** blow relative to CON:

- **Minor Wound** — below the Major Wound value (= CON). Painful but not disabling (several can still drop you below Unconscious).
- **Major Wound** — ≥ CON from one blow. The character **immediately goes unconscious**, checks Debilitated, and rolls once on **Table 11.1: Characteristic Lost** (lose 1 point, recompute derived stats). Any action before it fully heals causes Aggravation.
- **Mortal Wound** — ≥ Total Hit Points from one blow; usually kills. Survives only if **First Aid within one hour** restores them to ≥1 HP (Chirurgery can't help until then); then roll **three times** on Table 11.1.

### Table 11.1 — Characteristic Lost (1D6)

| 1D6 | Characteristic |
|-----|----------------|
| 1 | SIZ |
| 2 | DEX |
| 3 | STR |
| 4 | CON |
| 5 | APP |
| 6 | none |

## Unconscious

A character passes out at **HP ≤ Unconscious** or on any Major Wound (they may attempt an **Emergency Dismount** first). Check Debilitated. They may have brief lucid moments (whisper, dictate a will). Recovering above Unconscious or a successful Chirurgery restores faculties (though still Debilitated if applicable).

**Fighting beyond debilitation:** to keep fighting past Unconscious / after a Major Wound, make an unopposed **Energetic** roll **and** a roll vs **current HP** — both must succeed. Each round of fighting on costs **1 Aggravation** (acting with slow deliberation = −10 to all Skills but less Aggravation).

## Near Death

At **0 or negative HP** (any cause), the character dies at **midnight** unless **First Aid** restores them to positive HP that day (then Chirurgery is needed). The GM may rule that HP more negative than can be healed = instant death.

title: Horsemanship (Skill) + fumbling a Horsemanship roll
text:
## Horsemanship (Skill)

- **Categories:** Combat, Knightly, Ladies
- **Use:** Deed, Inquiry
- **Glory:** No

Feudal society is an equine society: horses are central to a knight's existence. **All noble men and women have this Skill** and begin learning it young, so **riding at any pace requires no roll** under ordinary conditions.

A Horsemanship roll is called for only in **difficult circumstances**, such as:
- Jumping ditches and hedges
- Racing, chasing, or covering long distances at speed
- Horse care and tending to unusual circumstances
- Riding side-saddle at a trot, canter, or gallop
- Appraising a horse's value, outfitting it properly, and anything else associated with horses
- **Contests** where competitors try to outdo each other, even in ordinary equine affairs

As an **Inquiry** skill it also supplies knowledge: e.g. to figure out the breed of a horse, roll Horsemanship.

**Not for training horses** — that is a separate Skill outside a knight's or lady's knowledge.

## Fumbling a Horsemanship roll

### General (Deed) fumble — printed p. 95
Horsemanship is a **Deed** skill (e.g. riding through difficult terrain). The general resolution outcomes apply:
- **Failure:** the character does not accomplish the deed.
- **Fumble:** the character does not accomplish the deed **and takes an experience check** to the Skill. The Gamemaster **may impose a negative modifier** to a follow-up resolution of relevant Traits, Passions, or Skills (e.g. a botched jump that scatters the hunt, unseats the rider, or spooks the horse into the next roll).

The specific bad thing that happens on a fumble is left to the GM and the situation; falling from the mount, injuring the horse, or losing a race are typical.

### Combat-specific fumbles
When Horsemanship is rolled inside the combat system, the dedicated fumble entries govern the result instead of the generic Deed rule:
- **Control Mount** fumble → rider is **thrown** (see [[core.combat.mounted-utility-actions]]).
- **Emergency Dismount** fumble → **2D6** damage, drop all weapons; a falling horse lands on the rider (Table 7.4, see [[core.combat.mounted-combat]]).
- **Mounted Lance Charge** fumble → Table 7.2 consequences (see [[core.combat.action-mounted-charge]]).

title: Fumbling a Horsemanship Roll — Consequences by Situation
text:
In the Pendragon RPG, fumbling a **Horsemanship roll** (rolling a natural 20, unless your skill is 20 or higher) is always highly dramatic, but the specific consequences depend entirely on the situation you are in:

### **1. General Riding & Inquiry Fumbles**

- **General Riding (Deed):** If you are attempting a difficult riding feat (such as jumping a hedge or racing) and fumble, you fail to execute the action. You do, however, gain an **experience check** to Horsemanship because we learn from our greatest mistakes. The Gamemaster may also apply a negative modifier to any follow-up actions.
- **Knowledge/Equine Appraisal (Inquiry):** If you roll Horsemanship to identify a horse's breed or appraise its value and fumble, you fail to retrieve the correct information, but still gain an experience check.

### **2. Controlling Mounts in Combat**

- **Non-Combat Trained Horses:** If you ride a normal riding horse (like a rouncy or palfrey) into battle, you must make a **Control Mount** roll at the start of each round at a -5 penalty. Fumbling this roll means **your knight is instantly thrown** and must immediately make an Emergency Dismount roll.
- **Wounded Horses:** If your horse takes 5 or more points of damage in combat, you must make a Horsemanship roll at the start of the next round with a penalty equal to the horse's lost Hit Points. Fumbling this means you are thrown.

### **3. Emergency Dismounts & Falling**

- **Emergency Dismount:** When your horse falls or you are about to be thrown, you roll Horsemanship to land safely. Fumbling this roll is catastrophic: **you take 2D6 falling damage** (dropping all held weapons), and if the horse itself has fallen, **it lands on top of you**, inflicting the horse's full normal Damage value (though armor protects against this latter damage normally).
- **Reducing Falling Damage:** Usually, when falling from a horse, a successful Horsemanship roll reduces your falling damage by 1D6 (2D6 on a critical). However, **fumbling this roll doubles the number of falling damage dice** you take.

### **4. Mounted Lance Charges**

- If you fumble a Mounted Charge with a couched spear or lance, your weapon breaks and you must roll Horsemanship to determine the disaster. Fumbling that follow-up Horsemanship roll means **your lance tip buries itself in the earth, bringing down both you and your horse; your lance is shattered, and you take 3D6 damage** which armor does not protect against.

### **5. Horse Care**

- If you are tending to a sick, injured, or overworked horse and fumble your Horsemanship roll, the animal becomes **terribly weak or sore**. For the long term, your horse suffers a **-2 penalty to its Horse Survival Roll** in the next Winter Phase, and you suffer a **-10 penalty to all Horsemanship rolls** until a farrier can tend to the mount.

### **6. Hunting & Obstacles**

- **Jumping Streams/Ditches:** Fumbling a Horsemanship roll to jump a small stream or ditch during a hunt causes **both you and your horse to fall, taking 1D6 damage**.
- **Squire Exercises:** If you are a young squire practicing turning after a charge and fumble, the **horse rears**. You must succeed at an unopposed DEX roll to stay in the saddle; failing means you fall for 1D6 damage and face the merciless laughter of your peers.

---

title: Skill Groups (Combat, Courtly, Knightly, Ladies, Woodcraft…)
text:
Skills are grouped by profession/setting; the groups overlap.

- **Combat** — Battle, Brawling, Charge, Horsemanship, all Weapon Skills.
- **Courtly** — Compose, Courtesy, Dancing, Falconry, Fashion, Flirting, Gaming, Intrigue, Literacy, Orate, Play (Instrument), Recognize, Religion, Singing. **Courtly Skill values are capped at the character's APP at creation** (they may rise above APP later).
- **Minsterly** (church/monastic) — Courtesy, Industry, Literacy, Orate, Religion (Christian), Singing.
- **Knightly** — Awareness, Battle, Brawling, Charge, Courtesy, First Aid, Horsemanship, Hunting, Recognize, all Weapon Skills. (Knighthood needs value 10 in Sword, Charge, Brawling + two non-weapon Knightly Skills.)
- **Non-Knightly** (forbidden to knights) — **Chirurgery, Industry**. Using them **diminishes Honor** and doesn't appear on a knight's sheet.
- **Ladies** — Chirurgery, Courtesy, Dancing, Fashion, First Aid, Horsemanship, Industry, Play (Instrument), Recognize, Singing, Stewardship.
- **Woodcraft** — Awareness, Bow, First Aid, Folklore, Hafted Weapons, Hunting, Spear, Stewardship.

Combined modifiers may never exceed **±20**.

title: Skill Uses — Deeds, Inquiry & Parlance
text:
Skills fall into one or more of three **uses**. Reserve rolls for when success/failure makes a meaningful difference.

## Deeds

Doing something specific, public, and important — make the relevant Skill/Combat Skill roll (opposed or unopposed).

- **Critical:** action done, take a check; GM may grant a **+ modifier** to a follow-up Trait/Passion/Skill roll.
- **Success:** action done; check only if significant.
- **Failure:** action not accomplished.
- **Fumble:** not accomplished, but take a check; GM may impose a **− modifier** to a follow-up roll.

## Inquiry

Accessing the body of knowledge a Skill implies (Sword → judge a blade's quality; Horsemanship → a horse's breed; Courtesy → what to do at a coronation). Usually an **unopposed** roll.

- **Critical:** knows a great deal (+check, + follow-up modifier).
- **Success:** knows enough (check if significant).
- **Failure:** can't recall the information.
- **Fumble:** doesn't know, but takes a check; GM may impose − modifiers — and may use **Secret Rolls** to conceal the fumble and feed false information.

## Parlance

Using a Skill to communicate/put others at ease, tailored to the audience: **Courtesy** with nobles, **Religion** with clergy, **Folklore** with commoners; **Orate** and (deceptively) **Intrigue** for persuasion. A Courtesy/Religion/Folklore roll may be made **before** an Orate/Intrigue roll to enhance it. Results mirror the above (critical/success/failure/fumble → communicated / not).

## Using a leader's Skills

Skills like **Battle** and **Hunting** may have a **leader** roll on behalf of a group (the followers must agree to follow, or rank decides). Only the leader rolls; followers get **no check**.

## Improving Skills

Skills increase permanently during the **Winter Phase** (field experience, training, practice, reputation, or supernatural means). See Ch.14.

title: Skills Defined (non-combat) — with Tables 5.1, 5.2 & 5.3
text:
Each entry lists **groups · use · Glory**. (Horsemanship: see [[core.skills.horsemanship]]; Weapon Skills: Ch.8.)

- **Awareness** — *Knightly, Woodcraft · Inquiry · No.* Spot/hear/notice things. Unopposed to scan, or opposed vs an active hider (Hunting for people, Avoidance for creatures). See condition modifiers below.
- **Battle** — *Combat, Knightly · Deed, Inquiry · Yes.* Lead or (alone) survive large-scale conflict. Knights fight in a **conroi** of 5–15 led by a banneret; the Skill is used by bannerets/commanders and by a lone cut-off knight. Full rules in the GM Handbook.
- **Chirurgery** — *Ladies, Non-knightly · Deed, Inquiry · No.* Keeps the debilitated from deteriorating so natural healing can work (heals nothing directly). **Forbidden to knights.** See Ch.11.
- **Compose** — *Courtly · Deed, Inquiry · Yes.* Create poems, ballads, songs.
- **Courtesy** — *Courtly, Knightly, Minsterly, Ladies · Inquiry, Parlance · No.* Knowledge of noble culture, laws, and etiquette; the parlance Skill for nobles.
- **Dancing** — *Courtly, Ladies · Deed, Inquiry · Yes.* Court dances.
- **Falconry** — *Courtly · Deed, Inquiry · Yes.* Hunt with raptors (a half/full-day activity); a good showing grants later Courtesy/Flirting modifiers at court.
- **Fashion** — *Courtly, Ladies · Deed, Inquiry · Yes.* Style; enhances **Geniality**. Needs time + funds paid a month ahead; judged publicly. A made outfit keeps its bonus **one year**, then decays one step/year. Dressing above your station risks a **Proud check** and reprimand.
- **First Aid** — *Knightly, Ladies, Woodcraft · Deed, Inquiry · Glory for saving a life* (10 knight / 25 banneret or famous / 50 baron or Round Table / 75 count-duke- petty king / 100 king or very famous RT / 250 High King). Immediate wound care; see Ch.11.
- **Flirting** — *Courtly · Deed, Inquiry, Parlance · No.* Romantic banter.
- **Folklore** — *Woodcraft · Inquiry, Parlance · No.* Commoner lore/customs; the parlance Skill for commoners.
- **Gaming** — *Courtly · Deed, Inquiry · Yes.* Play dice, chess, and other games well.
- **Hunting** — *Knightly, Woodcraft · Deed, Inquiry · No.* Track, pursue, and kill game; a leader may roll for the group.
- **Industry** — *Ladies, Minsterly, Non-knightly · Deed, Inquiry · No.* Craft cloth, clothing, textiles, and vestments (Table 5.3). **Knights lose 3 Honor each time they engage in it.**
- **Intrigue** — *Courtly · Inquiry, Parlance · Yes.* Learn court secrets and plots; subtle deceptive parlance.
- **Literacy** — *Courtly, Minsterly · Inquiry, Parlance · No.* Read and write a Language (starting value 0).
- **Orate** — *Courtly, Minsterly · Inquiry, Parlance · Yes.* Public speaking; sway crowds.
- **Play (Instrument)** — *Courtly, Ladies · Deed, Inquiry · Yes.* Musical performance.
- **Recognize** — *Courtly, Knightly, Ladies · Inquiry · No.* Identify knights, coats of arms, and families.
- **Religion** — *Courtly, Minsterly · Inquiry, Parlance · No.* Knowledge of one's faith; the parlance Skill for clergy.
- **Singing** — *Courtly, Minsterly, Ladies · Deed, Inquiry · Yes.* Vocal performance; hymns at mass.
- **Stewardship** — *Ladies, Woodcraft · Inquiry · No.* Land management (for land-holding knights). **+1 per Literacy 1–5, +2 per 6–10, etc.** Governs dispensing low justice on a manor.

## Awareness condition modifiers

Applied to Awareness (combined ≤ ±20):

- **Atmosphere** (fog/rain/smoke/snow): Light −5, Moderate −10, Heavy −15
- **Background noise:** Din −5, Clamor −10, Cacophony −15
- **Concealment:** Light −5, Moderate −10, Heavy −15
- **Darkness:** Dim (half-moon) −5, Shadowy (quarter) −10, Deep (new moon) −15, Complete −20
- **Light source (to spot in dark):** Torch +5, Campfire +10, Large campfire +15, Bonfire +20
- **Volume:** raised voices +5, shouting +10, trumpets +15 · **Taste:** additives −5

**Fire's light** removes penalties within its radius and reduces darkness one step out to double the radius: Bonfire 25 ft, Large campfire 15 ft, Campfire 10 ft, Torch 6 ft, Candle 3 ft.

title: Other Solos — Lost in the Woods, Madness & Pilgrimage
text:
## Lost in the Woods (Table 13.3)

A knight who becomes Lost is **Out of Game** and plays this Solo in the Winter Phase. **Once per season**, roll **Hunting** (regain the trail) and **Awareness** (spot a settlement) — each modifies the Table 13.3 roll by **+10 crit / +5 success / −5 failure / −10 fumble** — then roll **1D20 on Table 13.3**. Stop on a **Return Home** result; surviving all four seasons without one = lost another year.

Sample Table 13.3 results: low rolls = scarce food (lose 1 CON) or aimless wandering; mid = frightening beasts/bandits (flee, −5 next season); **malicious fairy** → gain **Fear (Fairies)** Obsession (and lose an eye / −5 Awareness, or roll on Table 14.4); high rolls = a villager, hunter, hermit, or wild man leads you home (with a relevant check). 20+ = reach the destination.

## Madness (Table 13.4)

A Maddened character passes to the GM, who rolls **once per year** on Table 13.4: Madness Activity until memory is restored, the Madness is cured, or the GM brings them back. Results range from shepherds/knights/hermits/Druids finding and healing them, to a unicorn's breath restoring their senses, to a malicious fairy holding them. (See [[core.traits-passions.afflictions]].)

## Pilgrimage

A religious journey to a distant holy site. Groups travel at the **slowest** pilgrim's pace (on foot = **half** Normal Rate). Bring funds for food, lodging, and alms. Visiting a **Royal City** (Table 13.5) or a **Great Lord** (Table 13.6) uses the same roll-then-check-Statistics structure as the Standard Activity Solo (no roll for a Passion you lack; both halves of a Trait pair can be checked).

After completing a pilgrimage, make an unopposed **Devotion (Deity)** roll (also checks Devotion):

- **Critical:** choose **3 Miracles**.
- **Success:** choose **1 Miracle**.
- **Failure:** no Miracle.
- **Fumble:** no Miracle and **no pilgrimages for 1D6 years**.

**Miracles list:** +1 to a Child or Horse Survival roll; +1D3 Healing Rate for a year; cure Disease/Poison (no longer Debilitated); cure Melancholy/Madness (if chaperoned/ bound); heal +1D3+3 HP; restore +1D2 to a Characteristic; or a story/plot miracle (GM's call).

**Sites:** Table 13.7 (Christian — e.g. Glastonbury Abbey, Canterbury, Salisbury Cathedral) and Table 13.8 (Pagan — e.g. Stonehenge, The Waters of Sulis, White Horses); each lists the Traits/Skills to check (always includes **Spiritual** and **Religion**).

title: Standard Activity Solos (Tables 13.1 & 13.2)
text:
Solo Scenarios **grant no direct Glory** and are optional. A player who **missed one or more game years** may run one Standard Activity Solo per missed year.

- **Step 1 — Find activity:** roll **1D20 on Table 13.1: Household Knight's Duties** for the year's dominant activity, which yields a set of **check rolls**. Also attend **Regular Court** (always: Courtesy, Hunting, Intrigue, Recognize, Religion; one religious Trait; Hospitality, Honor, Love (Person); + three chosen Courtly Skills).
- **Step 2 — Roll for checks:** roll each indicated Statistic; **success → check** (no penalty for plain failure). **Critical = 10 Glory.** A fumbled **Trait** roll checks the opposing Trait; a fumbled **Passion** roll loses 1 point; Skill fumbles carry no penalty. Only one check per Statistic (but you can check **both** halves of a Trait pair).

## Table 13.1 — Household Knight's Duties (1D20)

| 1D20 | Event | Check rolls / effect |
|------|-------|----------------------|
| 1–3 | Escort | Awareness, Courtesy, Horsemanship, Charge; Temperate/Indulgent; one Weapon Skill |
| 4–9 | Garrison & Patrol | Awareness, Courtesy, First Aid, Recognize; Honest/Deceitful; one Weapon Skill |
| 10 | Illness | CON roll; fumble → Table 14.4 (Characteristic Lost); a 6 there lets you take Training & Practice **twice** in Winter Phase |
| 11–13 | Tournament | Awareness, Horsemanship, Charge, Recognize, Sword; Generous/Selfish |
| 14–16 | Unusual Event | Roll on Table 13.2 |
| 17–18 | — | Roll twice, ignoring 17+ |
| 19–20 | — | Roll thrice, ignoring 17+ |

## Table 13.2 — Unusual Events (2D6)

2 Visit royal court · 3 Visit a lord's overlord · 4 Escort far (2+ counties) · 5–6 Escort nearby · 7–8 False alarm (reroll on 13.1) · 9–10 Local tournament · 11 Visit a lord's overlord · 12 Uprising among commoners.

Ask the GM what the **liege lord** did that year — a knight in service shares in those events (extra experience/Glory, GM's option).

title: Afflictions — Madness, Melancholy & Misery
text:
Afflictions arise from certain failed Passion rolls (see the Passion Crisis). All can be cured.

## Madness

A Maddened character is **Out of Game** — throws away weapons/armor, flees into the wilderness (or collapses catatonic); the player hands the sheet to the GM and runs a **Madness Solo** each Winter Phase while raving.

- **Glory:** 100 if it lasts a year or more, otherwise 25.
- **Curing:** only by someone who **Loves/Adores** the character, someone the character holds a Loyalty/Love/Adoration for, a **Famous/Exalted Merciful** person, a healing-professional monk/lady/hermit, or the **Holy Grail**. The healer succeeds a **Merciful** roll to calm them, then shelters and visits daily — **each month of care removes one year** of Madness duration; at 0 the mind clears (usually no memory of the episode). Madness lasting **under a month** must resolve on its own. Some enchanted wells/miracles/the Grail cure instantly.
- **Out-of-Game curing:** the GM may return the sheet at any time (adjusting Statistics to reflect the episode) — handy when the active character dies or goes Mad.

## Melancholy

A depressed state: **−5 to all Skill and Passion rolls**; incapable of normal action.

- **Glory:** 10. Effects wait until any current activity (e.g. a battle) finishes.
- **Value/duration:** equals a number of days (per Passion strength); left alone the **value drops 1/day**, then the character recovers. This value is the fixed opposition against a cure.
- **Friendly Cure:** someone with a Love/Loyalty/Adoration bond makes an **opposed Passion roll vs the Melancholy value** — win = lifted; partial = value −1, retry tomorrow; lose = the knight turns **violent** (→ Unfriendly Cure).
- **Unfriendly Cure:** being attacked snaps them out to defend themselves; combat (or a monk/lady's verbal assault/slap via a Cruel roll) continues until the healer is hurt or flees, or the Melancholic takes damage (which **ends** the affliction). One cure attempt per person per day.

## Misery

- **Becoming Miserable:** whenever an **Adoration** roll is failed (plus its other effects); or when Adoration is invoked away from the Beloved after Inspiration passes (if Impassioned via a critical, become **Melancholic** instead); the GM may also apply it on loss of a Love/Loyalty source. **Glory:** 10 (first time each year).
- **Effect:** **−2 to all Skills and Passions** until dispelled (stacks with other penalties).
- **Duration:** from a failed Adoration roll → ends 7 days after the following Sunday (or when cured); from loss of a loved one → weeks equal to the Passion's value.
- **Curing:** another person disturbs them with a successful **opposed Skill/Passion roll** (Intrigue, Orate; Merciful, Trusting; Homage, Loyalty (Companions), Chivalry, Duty (Vassals)) vs the causing Passion; a failed attempt triggers a Melancholy-style violent reaction. Also cured by seeing/hearing the Beloved.

title: Directed Traits & Obsessions (Avarice, Fear, Jealousy — Table 4.1)
text:
## Directed Traits

A **Directed Trait** is a feeling focused on a person/group that overrides the general attitude. Mark the Trait with an asterisk and note the object + modifier, e.g. `*Suspicious (King Mark) +5`. When rolling that Trait about its object, add the modifier **and reduce the opposing Trait by the same amount** (Trusting 14/Suspicious 6 becomes Trusting 9/Suspicious 11 vs King Mark).

- **Inherited:** starts at **half the parent's** value.
- **Voluntary:** usually **+1D6** (or as agreed).
- **GM-assigned:** usually **not more than +5**.
- **Raising:** with a check, roll higher than the current value in the Winter Phase to increase it by 1.

## Obsessions

A stronger Directed Trait that **always** affects actions. An **Obsession roll** is made each time the character encounters or hears about its object. Obsessions arise from unlucky rolls, GM ruling, or player request.

**Redemption:** (1) reduce it in the Winter Phase like a Passion; or (2) in the object's presence, make an **opposed Honor vs Obsession** roll (Table 4.1). An overweening Obsession can also be escaped by retiring to a monastery/hermitage (Out of Game for good).

### Table 4.1 — Obsession Resolution Results (Honor vs Obsession)

| Result | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| Critical | Overcome it — remove from sheet |
| Win | Partly overcome — **halve** its value |
| Tie | Attempt another opposed roll, or not (player's option) |
| Partial success | Reduce by 1 point |
| Loss | Waxes stronger — value **increases by half** |
| Fumble | Impossible to overcome — value **doubles** |

## The named Obsessions

- **Avarice** (extreme Selfish) — start **+2D6** to Selfish. Paths: fumble a Generous roll then succeed Selfish; **or** gain a Selfish critical bonus (GM picks the object). Effects: lacking the object causes **Misery** (once/day, crit or success → Misery); when a chance to obtain it arises, a Passion-style roll compels acquisition (critical = at any cost, morality aside).
- **Fear** (extreme Cowardly) — start **+1D6+5** to Cowardly. Paths: fumble a Valorous roll then succeed Cowardly; **or** GM/player decision. Effect: when confronted by the object, an unopposed Fear roll — success = refuse/withdraw to safety; critical = flee in terror at max rate until exhausted. Saves lives but costs Honor when fleeing is unbecoming.
- **Jealousy** (extreme Suspicious) — start **+2D6** to Suspicious. Paths include: fumble a Trusting roll then succeed Suspicious; fumble an obligatory Adoration roll; being publicly rebuffed by one's Adored (automatic); resentment of betters; Romantic Lovers must acquire a Jealousy of any threat to their Beloved. Effect: must try to **harm the Rival** (physically, socially, or via a Skill contest). In the Rival's company: **−5 to Forgiving, Just, Merciful, Prudent, Spiritual, and Trusting**.

title: The Passion Roll — Inspiration, Impassionment & Passion Crisis (Table 4.2)
text:
Most Passion rolls are **unopposed**. Each Passion may be used to **provoke a bonus only once per day** (rolls made purely to decide a course of action don't count against this limit).

## Table 4.2 — Unopposed Passion Roll Results

| Result | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| **Critical** | **Impassioned** — gain a check |
| **Success** | **Inspired** — gain a check |
| **Failure** | **Passion Crisis** (see below) |
| **Fumble** | Lose 1 point from the Passion |

- **Impassioned:** **+10** to a single Skill or Trait (player's choice) until the evoking situation ends (a duel until someone drops; a battle Skill bonus lasts one Battle Turn; may modify a series of First Aid/Chirurgery rolls from one trauma).
- **Inspired:** **+5** to a single Skill or Trait while the situation persists.

**Modifying Traits with Passions:** the Inspired/Impassioned bonus can be applied to a **Trait** to improve (or, by boosting an Unsung Trait, deliberately lower a Famous/ Exalted) Trait roll.

## Passion Crisis ("For Dole and Sorrow")

Triggered by a **failed** Table 4.2 roll — or when a character Inspired/Impassioned fails spectacularly at the task, or the Passion's source is lost/removed forever. Make an **unopposed roll against the triggering Passion** (+ modifiers):

- **Critical success → Madness** · **Success → Melancholy** · **Failure → no effect** · **Fumble → lose 1 point** from the Passion.

**Modifiers to that roll:** failed while Inspired **+0**; failed while Impassioned **+5**; currently Inspired by it **+5**; crisis due to own action/inaction **+10**; currently Impassioned by it **+10**.

**Affliction duration** (by unmodified Passion level):

| Level | Melancholic | Maddened |
|-------|-------------|----------|
| Unsung (1–4) | 1D6 hours | one week |
| Normal (5–15) | one day | 1D6 weeks |
| Famous (16–20) | 1D6 days | 1D6 months |
| Exalted (20+x) | 1D6 weeks | 1D6 years |

(Both may be healed before the duration ends — see [[core.traits-passions.afflictions]].)

## Internal Conflict

Passions may be used in **opposed** rolls to resolve inner conflict — usually a Passion vs a Trait. The player rolls both; the winner decides the action. (E.g. Hate (Saxons) 18 vs Merciful 12 over sparing civilians.)

title: Passions of Fervor, Adoratio & Civilitas (Love/Hate, Adoration/Devotion, Chivalry/Hospitality/Station)
text:
## Fervor — Love & Hate

Opposites; you cannot hold **both** Love and Hate for the same subject (though Hate (Cornishmen) + Love (Tristram the Cornishman) is fine). Their bonuses apply only to matters concerning the subject.

- **Hate (Person/Group)** — invoked on mere **awareness of proximity** (no contact needed), making Exalted Hates dangerous in peaceful settings. Choose the subject carefully — too broad brings constant grief, too narrow is useless. Restraint = opposed Hate vs another Passion/Trait (Homage, Chivalry; or Forgiving/Just/Merciful/ Trusting).
- **Love (Family)** — a **Universal Passion** every character has; invoked when family is endangered. (Family = immediate blood/adopted; Kin = extended; Lineage = common ancestor; Clan = close-knit related families.)
- **Love (Person)** — a tender/physical bond gained in play (GM may impose it). It is also the **successor to Adoration** once consummated, keeping the same value. Invoked when the subject is in danger.

## Adoratio — Adoration & Devotion

- **Adoration (Beloved)** — the chaste Passion of **fine amor / Romance**. The Beloved must be **apparently unattainable** and initially rejects the Lover; the Beloved's feelings don't matter — inspiration comes from their mere existence, and suffering deepens it. Two huge advantages: grants a **+10 Skill bonus regardless of Inspiration/Impassionment**, and may be invoked **once per day at any time for any reason**. May cause **Misery**; Famous/Exalted Adorers risk **Melancholy** at reminders of the Beloved. Requires complete chastity; **becomes Love if consummated** (moving to Fervor).
  - **Involuntary Adoration:** on first seeing someone of Transcendent Beauty/power (Ygraine, Guenever, Isoud, Lancelot, Tristram…), roll **Lustful, Arbitrary, and Honest** — if **all three succeed**, gain Adoration at **1D6** (+5 for Transcendent Beauty, +10 for exemplars like Guenever/Galahad). This is the only way to hold more than one Adoration at once.
- **Devotion (Deity)** — faith in a supernatural being; confers no knowledge or powers, and does **not** count as Directed. Acquired at will but **cannot inspire until the character qualifies as a Religious Knight** (p.127); then invoked at blasphemy, abuse of a holy place/person, or when championing the religion.

## Civilitas — Chivalry, Hospitality & Station

- **Chivalry** — the strong protect the weak; act honorably toward ladies, commoners, and knights. Generated by declaring the desire, but **cannot inspire until qualified as a Chivalrous knight**. May conflict with **Station** (resolve by opposed roll). Invoked when a chivalric virtue is offended or there's a chance to uphold the Code (defend a lady, protect a commoner). The Chivalric Code forbids e.g. missile weapons against knights and requires mercy (to deny a hated foe mercy needs a **failed Merciful roll**), generosity (sharing Glory with fellows), fairness, and courtesy.
- **Hospitality** — a Universal Passion; offer food/lodging/safety without expectation. Inside a hearth, **peace must reign** even between enemies, and a guest must help defend it; a guest may not leave without the host's permission, and the host may never act against a guest. Invoked by the wronged party when host or guest breaks Hospitality, or when a knight witnesses a violation. (Not invoked merely because your home is attacked from outside — but yes if an invited guest draws a weapon, or a permitted guest is attacked.)
- **Station** — a Universal Passion upholding the social order (king > nobles > knights > esquires > commoners). Invoked when witnessing offenses to station (a commoner failing deference, taking liberties, or offering violence to nobles; a protected commoner attacked by foreigners; a knight rebuked for abusing a commoner; a lower noble offending a higher). Knights **lose Honor** by behaving like commoners (manual labor, hawking goods, non-holding business). Chivalrous knights often make opposed rolls **against** their own Station.

title: Passions of Fidelitas (Duty, Fealty, Homage, Loyalty)
text:
Fidelitas is personal loyalty — always directed at a **person or group** (never a place, action, animal, artifact, or ideal). Bonds are sealed by oaths; oath-breakers become permanent outcasts.

- **Duty (Vassals)** — a lord's responsibility to their sworn knights; automatically gained whenever others swear Homage/Fealty to you. Invoked when a sworn vassal is in danger.
- **Fealty** — the "standard" feudal oath of obedience, sworn on Bible/relics, often **time-limited** and expiring without consequence; may be sworn to **multiple** lords; **inferior to Homage** (ignored if the two conflict). Mercenaries and professionals (stewards, clerks) swear Fealty for their term of service, then may serve anyone (even old enemies) without dishonor. Invoked when the lord is threatened or someone interferes with a deed done on his behalf.
- **Homage** — the **highest loyalty**, sworn for household membership or a land grant (heritable, if heirs also swear). One liege lord takes primacy over lesser homages. **Violating Homage is penalized more than any other loyalty — refusal loses Honor** (see [[core.aspirations.honor]]). Invoked when the liege or family is threatened, someone interferes with a deed for the lord, or the liege's Honor is impugned.
  - **Ending Homage/Fealty** never happens during a military expedition, only between wars: by *mutual agreement* (often generating a **Favor** to the releasing lord; a knight transferring up owes the new lord a Favor equal to the new Standard of Living); by *liege's choice* (needs serious cause; knight may demand trial by peers or combat); or by *knight's choice* (made public at court, returning gifts, declaring the lord's oath-violation; a resentful lord may name them enemy, granting **40 days' safe conduct**). A departing vassal keeps family lands but must quickly find a new liege or risk seizure.
- **Loyalty (Companions)** — mutual bond among a group of unrelated individuals (e.g. a band of PKs); list the members. Invoked when a companion is threatened, endangered, or fighting alongside.
- **Loyalty (King)** — loyalty to a king who isn't one's liege. If a vassal is more loyal to a king than their own lord, the lord may develop a **Jealousy** Obsession. It doesn't excuse feudal duty; escape requires formally breaking one's oath or being invited to serve the king directly. Invoked when the king/family is threatened, someone interferes with a deed for the king, or the king's Honor is impugned.

title: Passions — Nature, Levels, Courts, Raising/Lowering & Battle Use
text:
**Passions** are deeply-held beliefs/emotions that can inspire legendary feats or coerce a character against their interests. They may grant temporary modifiers to **Skills and Traits** — never to Characteristics or other Passions.

## Gaining a new Passion

Players may request one, or the GM may assign one when warranted (family murder → Hate; rescue → Loyalty; miracle → Devotion). A new Passion starts at **1D6+6** (GM may adjust). Too many Famous/Exalted Passions can cripple a knight (Lancelot's Love vs Homage).

## Passion levels

- **Unsung** 1–4 · **Normal** 5–15 · **Famous** 16–20 · **Exalted** 20+x.
- A **Famous** Passion triggers easily (less autonomy); an **Exalted** Passion must always be acted upon (rare).

## Courts (40-point cap each)

Passions belong to four courts — **Fidelitas, Fervor, Adoratio, Civilitas** — plus **Honor** (stands alone). **The sum of all Passions in a court may not exceed 40.** Raising one Passion in a full court forces another in that court **down** (player's choice), unless the rising one is already at 20.

**Directed Passions** are focused on a specific object (like Directed Traits). Devotion (Deity) explicitly does **not** count as Directed.

## Raising & lowering

- **Raise:** gain a check and roll above the value in the Winter Phase, or add a Prestige Reward.
- **Lower (permanent):** a fumbled Passion roll (−1); a fumbled Passion Crisis roll (−1); a Prestige Reward; court-cap displacement; or **deliberately violating** the Passion.

**Violating a Passion:** to act against its reason (secretly meeting your lord's enemy while holding Loyalty (Lord)) requires a **failed Passion roll** and reduces the Passion by 1. Exalted Passions can't be failed this way unless modifiers drop them below 20.

## Passions in battle

Each Passion may inspire **once per battle** (multi-day battles like Badon may allow more). A knight does **not** get Homage/Loyalty (King) merely because their liege is present — only if the liege is in **immediate danger**. When to roll **Hate** depends on the enemy army's composition (vs a Saxon army, a Famous/Exalted Hate (Saxons) lets the knight choose the round; vs Saxon mercenaries in a Cymric army, it must be rolled on first contact).

**GM characters** generally don't use Passions early on, but should later in a campaign and whenever a nameless knight defends their own home/liege.

title: Traits & Trait Rolls (Decision/Test/Hint, Valorous Roll, Religious Virtues)
text:
Traits are paired emotions (summing to 20) that influence Honor, Glory, and behavior. A character tends to act on the higher Trait. **Normal (5–15)** Traits allow the most freedom; **Famous (16–20)** and **Exalted (20+x)** Traits increasingly compel behavior. A critical or fumble on a Trait roll may grant a **+5 to a subsequent Skill or Passion roll**.

## Trait Roll results

Roll 1D20 against the Trait. Famous/Exalted Traits **must be rolled first**; an unmodified Exalted Trait never fails.

- **Critical** — acts strongly per the Trait; take a check; GM may grant +5 to a later Skill/Passion roll.
- **Success** — acts per the Trait; check only if significant.
- **Failure** — roll again against the **Opposing Trait** (with modifiers). If that also fails, the player acts as they wish.
- **Fumble** — acts strongly per the **Opposing Trait** and checks it; GM may grant the +5.

**Opposing Trait roll:** Critical → acts strongly per opposing Trait (+check, +5); Success → acts per opposing Trait; Failure → player's choice; Fumble → acts strongly per the **original** Trait (+check, +5).

Modifiers apply to the Trait value (large/horrifying creatures often impose −Valorous; this can drop an Exalted Trait below 20, forcing a roll).

## Trait Rolls in Play (three ways)

- **Decision rolls** — decide behavior. Not truly opposed: if the first roll succeeds, the second isn't made. Player picks which side to test first (except a Famous Trait must be tested first if acting against it; an Exalted Trait offers no choice).
- **Test rolls** — unopposed moral/spiritual trials (a *Just* roll to answer a justice riddle; an *Indulgent* roll to avoid getting drunk). Some tests just compare the **value** (Honest 15+ to reach Avalon; a shield only an Exaltedly Chaste knight may bear).
- **Game hint rolls** — GM prompts ("Suspicious characters get a roll here"); success = check, and an Opposing Trait roll follows a failure.

## Influencing another character

An **opposed Trait vs Trait** roll. If the influencer wins, the target takes an automatic check in the influencing Trait; if the influencer loses, they make an immediate Opposing Trait roll for a check. The winning Trait dictates the action; a tie is no result. This can **diminish another's Famous/Exalted Trait**.

**Traits opposing Passions:** a Trait may oppose a Passion (own or another's) via an opposed roll; the loser may make an Opposing Trait roll for a check.

## The Valorous Roll

A fairy or beast with a **Valorous Modifier** cannot be attacked until the character makes a **Valorous roll** (a Test Roll — everyone rolls, even Unsung/Normal), adjusted by the modifier, on sighting it. **Fail** → hesitate one Combat Round, may retry. **Fumble** → flee the scene.

## Religious Virtues (16+ in all six → Religious Knight boon, p.127)

- **Christian:** Chaste, Forgiving, Merciful, Modest, Spiritual, Temperate
- **Pagan:** Energetic, Generous, Honest, Lustful, Proud, Spiritual
- **Wodinic:** Generous, Indulgent, Proud, Reckless, Valorous, Worldly
- **Heathen:** Arbitrary, Honest, Proud, Spiritual, Suspicious, Vengeful

title: Coinage & Sources of Treasure
text:
Coins are rare until after the Conquest Period; non-lordly knights mostly barter, but goods have money-equivalent values (a vassal knight's £10 annual income comes as food and labor, not coin).

## Coins

- **Librum (£)** — gold; **£1 = 240d.** Mostly a **unit of account** (household knights rarely see gold).
- **Denarius (d.)** — silver penny; the usual cash. **1d. = £1/240.**

**£1 equivalences:** a peasant family's yearly support; a squire + two horses for a year; a feast for 30 nobles (or 100 commoners); a scholar's annual upkeep. **1d.:** a knight's meal; three crossbow bolts; a monk reading a letter aloud.

## Sources of treasure

Land is the most desired wealth; otherwise **ransom** is the most common income (see [[core.wealth.ransom]]), plus **loot** (portable coin/treasure for various actions).

title: Favors (Table 12.6)
text:
Feudal society runs on reciprocity: a great service creates an **owed Favor** between nobles. No contract is needed — **failing to repay loses Honor equal to the Favor's value**. Favors may be repaid by deed, coin, loan of a servant, or anything of value, in part or whole. Written as **F**value in the sheet's History & Events. **F1 ≈ an act worth 10 Glory, or a gift worth £1.**

## Table 12.6 — Favor Value Synopsis

| Value | Act |
|-------|-----|
| **F1** | £1 of goods; £1 annual land value; an act granting 10 Glory; education enough for a Skill check; a skilled servant's service for one year |
| **F10** | An act tied to **1 point of Honor** gain/loss |
| **×10** | If the deed repeats **for life** (land gifts, lifetime service) |
| **×20** | If the yearly deed is **inheritable** (land grants) |

- **Land grants:** ×20 only within a day's ride; adjacent regions (Cambria, Cumbria) = **×10**; two regions distant / Ireland / the Continent = **×2**.
- **Saving a family member, servant, or warhorse** = **one-tenth** of their ransom/value (higher if a notable Passion is held for them). E.g. saving an £8 charger → F1 (rounded up from 0.8).

title: Price Lists & Supporting Characters (Squires, Table 12.7)
text:
Knights avoid cash transactions (the province of merchants); when an item is **given**, use its market value to set the Favor owed. Items under £1 are acquired more or less automatically. **Royal mints** are the only coin source.

## Representative prices (Boy King Period)

- **War horses:** Hobby £2 · Small Charger £4 · Charger £8. **Riding:** Inferior Rouncy 120d. · Rouncy £1 · Large Rouncy £1½ · Jennet/Courser £2. **Work:** Sumpter 120d. · Mule/Donkey 60d. (see [[core.horses.types-and-stats]] for training/color surcharges).
- **Weapons:** Cheap Sword 60d. · Seax 40d. · Club 20d. · Cudgel/Quarterstaff 10d. · Bow 30d. · Light Crossbow 60d. · Francisca 15d. · Javelin 10d.
- **Armorer:** Scutum 30d. · Simple Shield/Targe 10d. · Half Gambeson (horse) 120d. · Full Gambeson (horse) £1 · Full Plain Caparison 90d.
- **Gear:** Travel Gear (½ horse-load) 120d. · War Gear (one pack-horse load, incl. travel) £1.

## Supporting characters — Squires

A squire owns only clothes, a knife, bowl, spoon, and blanket (the knight provides all else). A knight may keep **up to three** squires at arms (£1/year each for upkeep + a horse); the first is the **Body Squire** with authority over the others.

- **Skills:** a needed Skill value defaults to **5**, except Horsemanship, Brawling, Charge, Sword, and one non-weapon Skill, which start at **current age − 9** (± Table 12.7). **Homage (Lord) begins at 15.**
- **Starting age:** roll 1D20 — **14 or less → age 14**; **15+ → that age**. Knighted or released as an esquire at **21**.

### Table 12.7 — Squire Background Modifiers

| 1D20 | Background | Squire Skill | Knightly Skills |
|------|-----------|--------------|-----------------|
| 1–5 | Son of an esquire | −2 | −1 |
| 6–10 | Younger son of a vassal knight | −1 | 0 |
| 11–15 | Second son of a vassal knight | 0 | 0 |
| 16–20 | Heir of a vassal knight | +2 | +1 |
| GM fiat | Child of a holy man | −4 | −2 |
| GM fiat | Child of a commoner | −7 | −3 |

title: Ransom (Tables 12.1–12.5)
text:
Captured knights buy freedom with a **ransom** paid to the captor — a key reason knights spare each other. Lords ransom household knights; mercenaries supply their own (or their families); landed knights collect from their vassals. **Rule of thumb: ransom = the person's normal income/maintenance.**

- **Surrender oath:** a surrendering knight swears **not to escape** (Honor binds them).
- **Nobles** always become the **king's property**; Arthur pays about **half** the value.
- **Sharing:** captors divide the ransom as they agree (helping GM characters get a share).
- **Collecting:** prisoners stay captive until paid — chained, free-roaming, or released on their **word of honor** to return with funds (or back to captivity within **a year and a day**). A **ransom broker** pays **50%** at once and takes over the claim.
- **Tribal cultures** recognize ransom, but hatred often means the captive is killed or enslaved instead.

## Ransom values

**Table 12.1 — Knights:** Squire £1 · Mercenary Esquire £2 · Mercenary Knight £3 · Household Knight £4 · Vassal (Poor Manor) £8 · Vassal (Normal) £10 · Vassal (Multiple Manors) £20+ · Banneret £100.

**Table 12.2 — Nobles:** Baron £300 · Rich Baron £600 · Count/Duke/Petty King £1,000 · King/independent ruler £3,000.

**Table 12.3 — Soldiers:** Spearman/Swordsman/Archer 60d. · Guardsman 120d. · Leader of 10 120d. · Leader of 100 £1 · Cavalryman £2 · Leader of 1,000 £4.

**Table 12.4 — Clergy:** Lay Member 120d. · Priest/Monk/Canon £1 · Bishop/Abbot £300 · Archbishop £2,000.

**Table 12.5 — Tribal:** *Saxons* — Ceorl none, Heorthgeneat £2, Thegn £4, Ætheling £40, King £400. *Picts* — Warrior none, Chieftain £2. *Irish* — Kern none, Bonnacht £2, Chieftain £20.

title: Table 8.1 — Melee & Brawling Weapons
text:
**Damage** is the character's Damage Statistic ("Character") or Brawling Damage ("Brawling"), plus any listed bonus; "Horse" = the mount's Charge Damage. **Long** weapons get +5 charging a foe without one. Unless noted, non-sword melee weapons **break on a fumble or on a tie vs a sword-wielder**.

| Weapon | Skill | Foot/Mtd | Damage | Notes |
|--------|-------|----------|--------|-------|
| Arming Sword | Sword | Both | Character | **Parry +3**; breaks other weapons on a tie; **does not break on a fumble** |
| Battle Axe | Hafted | Both | Character\* | \*strikes through shields |
| Club | 2H Hafted | Foot | Brawling +2D6 | no shield |
| Cudgel | Hafted | Both | Brawling +1D6 | — |
| Francisca | Hafted | Foot | Brawling +2D6 | — |
| Great Axe | 2H Hafted | Foot | Character +2D6\* | no shield; \*strikes through shields |
| Great Mace | 2H Hafted | Foot | Character +2D6 (**+3D6 vs mail**) | no shield |
| Javelin | Spear | Both | Brawling +1D6 | — |
| Lance | Charge | Mounted | Horse | Long weapon |
| Lance, Jousting | Charge | Mounted | Horse | Long weapon; **rebated** (blunt); breaks on a **successful odd-numbered** Charge roll |
| Mace | Hafted | Both | Character (**+1D6 vs mail**) | — |
| Maul | 2H Hafted | Foot | Character +2D6 | no shield |
| Quarterstaff | Spear / Sword / 2H Hafted | Foot | Brawling (Spear); Brawling +2D6 (Sword); Brawling +1D6 (2H Hafted) | Parry +2 (Sword) / +4 (2H Hafted); no shield with Sword/2H |
| Spear | Spear | Both | Character (+2D6 if two-handed) | Long weapon; no shield if two-handed |
| **Dagger** | Brawling | Both | Brawling +2D6 | Close Quarter |
| **Seax** | Brawling | Foot | Brawling +2D6 | Parry +1 |

**\* Axes vs shields:** when a Battle/Great Axe hits a shielded opponent, the **shield blocks only 1D6** (never more than its Protection Value); a **roll of 1 breaks** the shield permanently.

## Rebated (blunted) weapon damage

A rebated weapon deals **half the rolled damage** on a successful action. A **critical adds +4D6 first, then the total is halved.** Always use the **full** rolled damage for **Knockdown**. (Combines with the Withhold Damage action: reduce dice, compute Knockdown, then halve for damage.)

title: Table 8.2 — Missile & Thrown Weapons
text:
Bows deal the character's own Weapon Damage **−1D6**, but each is **capped** regardless of the wielder (a 5D6 character with a longbow deals 4D6; only 3D6 with a self bow). Ranges are detailed under Missile Ranges (p.152; see [[core.combat.missile-weapons]]).

## Table 8.2 — Missile weapons

| Weapon | Skill | Foot/Mtd | Damage | Range |
|--------|-------|----------|--------|-------|
| Crossbow, Light | Crossbow | Both (must be on foot to load) | 1D6+10 | Medium |
| Self Bow | Bow | Both | Character −1D6, **max 3D6** | Medium |
| Longbow *(Cambrians)* | Bow | Foot | Character −1D6, **max 4D6** | Long |
| Warbow *(Cambrians)* | Bow | Foot | Character −1D6, **max 5D6** | Long |

## Table 8.2 — Thrown weapons

| Weapon | Skill | Foot/Mtd | Damage | Range |
|--------|-------|----------|--------|-------|
| Dagger | Thrown Weapon | Both | Brawling | Short |
| Francisca | Thrown Weapon | Both | Character −1D6 (**regular Damage vs shielded opponents**) | Short |
| Javelin | Thrown Weapon | Both | Character −1D6, max 3D6 | Medium |
| Spear | Thrown Weapon | Both | Character −1D6 | Short |

## Notes

- **Longbow** — a hunting bow; only a wielder with the **Bow Skill and STR** draws it fully (others treat it as a self bow).
- **Warbow** — needs **Bow Skill and STR each ≥ 15** to draw fully (else a self bow).
- **Crossbow, Light** — a "one-foot" crossbow; braced with a foot in the stirrup to load.
- **Thrown dagger** — awkward in flight and unlikely to strike home (specialized throwing daggers appear later).
- A **spear** may be thrown but less effectively than a javelin (shorter range).

title: Rebated (Blunted) Damage and How It Interacts with Criticals
text:
**Yes, rebated damage rules absolutely apply to a critical hit**, and the Pendragon rules outline exactly how the two mechanics interact:

1. **Add the Critical Bonus First:** When you land a critical hit, you add the standard **+4D6 damage bonus** to your weapon's base damage roll.
2. **Determine Knockdown Using Full Damage:** Before halving anything, you use the **full, unhalved rolled damage total** to determine if your opponent is knocked down. This makes rebated weapons excellent for unseating opponents without killing them.
3. **Halve the Total for Actual Damage:** Once the knockdown check is resolved, you **halve the entire rolled damage total** (the base damage plus the +4D6 critical bonus) to calculate the actual damage points inflicted on the target.

### **Example in Play**

If a knight with a base Weapon Damage of 4D6 lands a critical hit with a rebated arming sword:

- They roll **8D6** (4D6 base + 4D6 critical bonus).
- If the dice total **30 points of damage**:
    - The opponent must check for **Knockdown against the full 30 points** (compared against their SIZ).
    - The actual damage applied to the opponent is halved, meaning they take **15 points of damage** before subtracting their armor and shield protection.

---
