title: Weapon Skills, Parry Protection & Breakage
text:
Each melee Weapon Skill covers a **suite** of related weapons — you fight equally well with any weapon under the same Skill (switch a battle axe for a mace mid-fight, both **Hafted**; but a sword uses **Sword**). Every knight must master **Charge, Sword, and Brawling**. **All Weapon Skills default to DEX/2** at creation (from DEX at 14).

## The Skills

- **Charge** — used *instead of* the weapon's own Skill when mounted and moving fast enough for a **Mounted Charge** (p.140); its value supersedes the wielded weapon's. Never for bare hands / Brawling weapons. Charging with a **Long** weapon vs a foe without one gives **+5**. **Lances** are the only weapons used exclusively with Charge.
- **Sword** — any long-bladed weapon, one or two hands. No notable strengths/weaknesses; the most generally effective type and the symbol of knighthood.
- **Spear** — long-hafted stabbing weapons in close combat, one or two hands. Versatile but fragile: **all spears break on a fumble or on a tie vs a sword-wielder**. Throwable ones also use Thrown Weapon.
- **Hafted / Two-Handed Hafted** — axes, maces, hammers (one/two hands). Advantages vary by type; break on a fumble or on a tie vs a sword.
- **Flail** — the war flail (post-Boy King) needs its own Skill; two-handed (**no shield**); breaks on fumble/tie-vs-sword.
- **Brawling** — fists, wrestling, knives/daggers at Close Quarters/Contact, all Brawling actions and improvised weapons.
- **Bow** — wood/horn missile weapon; knights use it for hunting, not usually combat.
- **Crossbow** — any crossbow; needs far less training than a bow.
- **Thrown Weapon** — any thrown implement (spears, javelins, daggers, axes, stones).

## Parry Protection

Swords and some two-handed weapons give **Parry +x** (x = 2–4) when used without a shield — works like Shield Protection: a **Partial Success** triggers the bonus to Armor Protection. **Shield and Parry Protection cannot both apply to the same attack.**

A **secondary off-hand weapon** (instead of a shield) grants **+2 Parry Protection** (or **+1** if the main hand holds a sword), on top of the main weapon's Parry; it **cannot be used offensively**.

## One-handed weapons, shields & handedness

Knights usually pair a one-handed weapon with a shield. Without a shield, a one-handed weapon may be gripped in two hands but **does not gain the +2D6** of a true two-handed weapon (GM may rule such a two-handed grip avoids dropping the weapon on a fumble). All combatants are trained **right-handed** (a lone left-hander ruins close formation).

title: Ranks of Knighthood (Table 1.1) & Mercenary Pay (Table 1.2)
text:
Not all knights are equal. **About three in five** are mercenary or household knights; **almost two in five** are vassal knights holding land from the king or a great lord; **one in fifty** is a **banneret** — a lord without title who holds **at least ten other knights in vassalage**.

==A banneret's children do not inherit the rank.== It is earned in battle, and **only the king** may confer it, on his most trusted and valorous companions.

At **age 21** squires are free from service. Those destined for knighthood swear to uphold their duties and take an oath under a new lord. Squires who are heirs to property — usually first-born sons — become knights; younger offspring are not guaranteed the honor.

## Table 1.1 — Knight Ranks

| | Mercenary | Household | Vassal | Banneret |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Leader** | None | Liege Lord | Liege Lord | Liege Lord |
| **Loyalty Passion** | Fealty | Homage | Homage (Fealty) | Homage (Fealty) |
| **Term of service** | Varies | For life | For life | For life |
| **Equipment replacement** | Self | Liege Lord | Self | Self |
| **Who pays ransom** | Self | Liege Lord | Tenants | Tenants and vassals |
| **Followers** | None | Squire | Squire, foot soldiers, (knights), garrison | Squires, knights, foot soldiers, garrison |
| **Spouse** | Very rarely | Sometimes | Yes | Yes |
| **Marriage requirements** | Family consent | Liege Lord's permission | Liege Lord's preference | Liege Lord's preference |

## The Mercenary Knight

A hard life. The mercenary took the rank of knight but entered nobody's permanent service — typically a second-born whose elder sibling inherits everything, or the fourth or fifth child of a knight wealthy enough to confer the status.

He lives by his wits as a hired killer. If he has a servant it is **not usually a squire** (too extravagant) but a groom or lackey, who is not a battlefield follower. His equipment is rarely the latest type, his horses are smaller, and his clothes are often unfashionable or ragged. ==His kit deteriorates at **half its value per year**, and there is no liege lord to replace it.==

**The Indenture.** Mercenaries swear homage to no liege lord, only **temporary fealty**, committing to whichever commander offers a contract — an **indenture** specifying the term of service and rate of pay. It is written out and **cut in two halves along a zigzag**, one for the commander and one for the knight; if the terms are disputed the two pieces are matched to prove them originals.

## Table 1.2 — Mercenary Pay

| Pay rate | Foot Soldier | Archer | Mounted Cavalry | Knight |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **d. per day** | ½ | 1 | 2 | 4 |
| **d. per month** | 10 | 20 | 40 | 80 |
| **d. per season** | 30 | 60 | 120 | 240 |
| **£ per year** | ½ | 1 | 2 | 4\* |

\* **Proven knights are paid more than unknown ones**, earning a bonus by Glory: **Notable** knights up to an extra **£1** per year, **Renowned** knights **£2**. On reaching **Illustrious** Glory a mercenary commands up to an extra **£4**, and his lord will often invite him to become a household knight.

title: Winter Phase — Economic Circumstances & Aging (Steps 4–5)
text:
## Step 4 — Economic Circumstances

Set by last year's **Standard of Living**.

- **Impoverished:** lose squire, horses, and **2 Honor**; −1 to child-survival (worsening yearly); immediate **−1 SIZ/STR/APP** (cumulative, restored after a year Ordinary+); all armor **−1 permanently per year**; a CON roll or lose 1 CON; clothing halved; childbirth **−3**.
- **Poor:** horses & children **−1** survival; each horse loses 10 Move, 3 CON, 1D6 Charge damage; immediate −1 SIZ/STR/APP (+ CON roll); armor **−1**; clothing halved.
- **Income:** a vassal knight nets ~**£1 discretionary** from £10 lands (£6 maintenance, £3 soldiers/servants). Household knights get maintenance from their lord (often +£1 at Yule).
- **Maintenance (Table 14.2):** household knights are kept at **Ordinary** (£4 bachelor / £6 married); mercenary/vassal knights **choose** how much to pay for next year's Standard of Living. **Raising emergency coin:** call in a Favor (F1 = £1) — a vassal asking his liege owes **F1 per £1**.

## Step 5 — Aging & Old Age

Age +1 each Winter Phase. From **age 35**, check **Senescence** and **Infirmity** yearly.

**Senescence:** roll **2D6 on Table 14.3: Aging** for the number of rolls on **Table 14.4: Characteristic Lost**.

| 2D6 | Characteristics affected |
|-----|--------------------------|
| 2 / 12 | 4 |
| 3 / 11 | 3 |
| 4 / 10 | 2 |
| 5 / 9 | 1 |
| 6–8 | 0 |

**Table 14.4 — Characteristic Lost (1D6):** 1 SIZ (stooping) · 2 DEX (palsy) · 3 STR (weakness) · 4 CON (illness) · 5 APP (deformation) · 6 none. Recompute derived stats on each loss. (Also used for Major/Mortal wounds, magic, madness, etc.)

- **Infirmity:** when any Characteristic **other than CON reaches 5**. The character **retires** (turns title/lands/arms to the heir, keeps remaining Passive Glory). Aging losses at 5 or below are taken from **CON** instead (the rolled stat stays at 5).
- **Decrepitude:** when **CON reaches 5** — bedridden, out of play, no more Glory; still ages. Each year roll **1D6 vs CON**: higher than CON = death.
- **Death:** a failed Decrepitude Roll, or **CON 0**.

title: Winter Phase — Family & Childbirth (Step 11, Tables 14.8–14.12)
text:
Step 11 resolves the year's **births and deaths** (the event may have happened any time; it's determined now). A Prestige Reward may guarantee a healthy birth or a child's gender (own children only).

## Conception & childbirth

When conception is possible, the woman rolls **CON** (assume CON 13 if unspecified) with modifiers: **−10** if she had a child last year; **−X** per year over 35; **−1** Poor; **−1 per year** Impoverished. If modified CON ≤ 0 or the marriage is barren, don't roll.

- **Critical:** roll 1D6 — 1–4 **Multiple Birth** (Table 14.11); 5 Blessed Birth boy; 6 Blessed Birth girl (Table 14.12).
- **Success:** healthy child (boy on an odd roll, girl on even).
- **Failure:** no conception.
- **Fumble:** if a child was born last year, none this year; otherwise **Tragedy** (Table 14.8).

### Table 14.8 — Tragedy (1D6, +1 if first conception)

| 1–2 | Mother and child die |
| 3–4 | Mother dies, healthy child born |
| 5 | Mother now barren, healthy child born |
| 6 | Mother now barren, child dies |
| 7 | No child, barren marriage |

**PC childbirth (better odds):** on a Tragedy, the mother's player may fight for life — **CON** roll (live, −1 CON; else −2 and try **STR**), then **STR** (live, −1 STR; else −2 and try **SIZ**), then **SIZ** (live, −1 SIZ; else dies). **Midwifery:** a Wisewoman's successful Midwife roll may alter one death outcome (not a barren result).

Sons inherit the **father's** Family Characteristic; daughters the **mother's**.

## Survival & special births

- **Table 14.9 — Child Survival:** age 1 dies on **1–4**; ages 2–5 die on **1** (else healthy). Impoverished **−2**, Poor **−1**. **Table 14.10 — Cause of Death (1D6):** 1–3 illness, 4–5 accident, 6 missing/presumed dead.
- **Table 14.11 — Multiple Birth:** 1–7 boy+girl twins; 8–10 fraternal girls; 11–13 fraternal boys; 14–16 identical girls; 17–19 identical boys; 20 triplets.
- **Table 14.12 — Blessed Birth:** never rolls for survival (guaranteed to adulthood) and grants a bonus — e.g. +1 CON/APP/DEX/STR, or +5 to a Skill (Awareness, Compose, Horsemanship, Orate, etc.).

title: Winter Phase — Steps, Personal Events & Experience Rolls
text:
The annual **Winter Phase** has 11 steps: **1** Solo Scenario · **2** Personal Events · **3** Experience Rolls · **4** Economic Circumstances · **5** Aging & Old Age · **6** Squire & Maiden-in-Waiting · **7** Horse Survival · **8** Training & Practice · **9** Tally Glory · **10** Prestige Reward · **11** Family.

## Step 1 — Solo Scenario

Run any applicable Solo first (especially for a missed game year) to acquire checks. See [[core.solo-scenarios.standard-activity-solos]].

## Step 2 — Personal Events (Table 14.1)

Roll **1D20 on Table 14.1: Personal Events** for a tested Trait/Passion, then make an unopposed roll against it:

- **Critical:** make an immediate experience roll (Step 3) for it **and** check it.
- **Success:** check it.
- **Failure:** (Trait) roll the opposite and check if successful.
- **Fumble:** (Trait) check the opposite; (Passion) lose 1 point.

(Roll 20 = player's choice of Trait/Passion.)

## Step 3 — Experience Rolls

For **each experience check** on the sheet, **roll 1D20**: if the roll is **greater than the current value**, the Statistic **increases by 1**. A value at **20 (with or without a critical bonus) requires a 20** to raise. **One roll per checked Statistic per year**; all checked Statistics are rolled. (The higher the value, the less likely it grows.)

title: Winter Phase — Squires, Horses, Training, Glory & Prestige (Steps 6–10)
text:
## Step 6 — Squire & Maiden-in-Waiting

Everyone ages +1. Squires are released at **21** (become esquires). An attached esquire (£1/yr) may leave: roll **1D20 vs (years served past 20 + 5)** — success = departs. **Maidens (Table 14.5):** roll 1D20 (**20+ = marries and departs**); +2 per year of service 17–20, +5 per year past 20. Other Supporting Characters check **Table 14.6: Departure** (1 death, 2 depart, 3 depart, 4–20 stay).

## Step 7 — Horse Survival (Table 14.7)

Roll **1D20 for each charger, destrier, or unique horse** (household knights' ordinary sumpters/rouncys are replaced automatically to a minimum stable of 1 charger, 2 rouncys, 1 sumpter):

| 1D20 | Result |
|------|--------|
| ≤1 | Horse dies/unusable (not even sellable) |
| 2 | Roll Horsemanship: crit = healthy; success = **Weakened** (−2 Move, −1D6 HP, −1 to future survival rolls); failure = double those + −1D6 Charge damage; fumble = dies |
| 3–20 | Healthy |

## Step 8 — Training & Practice (pick one)

- **Trait:** +1 (opposite −1; min 1); **no Trait above 19**; no critical bonus.
- **Passion:** +1 or −1; **max 20**; no critical bonus; court 40-cap displacement applies.
- **Characteristic:** +1 to STR/DEX/CON/APP (**not after age 35**; SIZ only via Getting Fat).
- **Skills up to 15:** distribute **6 points** among Skills under 15 (none over 15).
- **A Skill up to 20:** raise one Skill over 15 by **+1** (max 20; no critical bonus).

**Getting Fat:** SIZ may be raised 3 times after 21, each adding a feature — 1st Heavyset; 2nd Portly (−1 DEX); 3rd Obese (−1 DEX, −1 CON). Obese characters pay more for fitting, may be too heavy for small horses, and gain **20 Passive Glory/year**.

## Step 9 — Tally Glory

Sum all Glory from the year (including Winter Phase) into Total Glory. **Passive Glory** accrues from annual benchmarks; adventures/quests/challenges are the primary source.

## Step 10 — Prestige Reward

**One per full 1,000 Glory**, spendable only in the Winter Phase (may be saved):

- Raise **any Statistic +1** (no restrictions; may add/raise a Skill critical bonus over 20).
- Lower a Passion by 1.
- Guarantee an **heir** conceived, healthy, and of chosen gender — or the conception/ health/gender of any child.

If a Trait/Passion reaches 16 (or an Ideal qualifies) **via** a Prestige Reward, the corresponding Passive Glory waits until next year, but the **bonuses apply immediately**.

title: Accommodations — Where Travelling Knights Sleep
text:
Travelling knights stay at **any castle, manor, monastery, or settlement** they come across. **Hospitality is an honored tradition**: the custom is to help any traveler appropriate to their status.

Most people travel very little and are **starved for news and gossip**, so non-threatening strangers are welcome — and more welcome still if they are entertaining.

> **If an enemy comes to the door**, the porter simply **stalls**, perhaps trading bitter or insulting words with the travelers, while the household's knights **take up arms and prepare to rush out and capture them**.

## By type of lodging

- **Monasteries** welcome all guests. Grooms attend the horses; guests are given a place to clean up and rest. **Separate quarters by social rank** keep nobility apart from commoners; higher nobility and **Round Table Knights may be offered the abbot's own quarters**. Commoners get austere monkish fare, while **knights and nobles eat richer victuals at the abbot's table**.
- **Peasant dwellings**, where nothing better exists. Commoners are ==usually reluctant to admit powerful strangers== and may recommend someone in town who is "less suspicious". An agreeable host tentatively accepts, then complains he is poor with nothing to spare and hints at compensation. **They dicker until a price is agreed — nothing is guaranteed except what both parties agree.**
- **Public inns do not exist yet.** They appear only in the **late Tournament Period**, first in cities and market towns, and are initially poor: no private accommodation, no menu, no food beyond common peasant fare, and everyone housed in **one large common room with a single fireplace**.
- **Camping.** If nothing can be found, knights sleep on the cold, hard ground — those travelling with **fine pavilions** find it more tolerable.

title: Captivity — Surrender, the Oath of Parole & Collecting a Ransom
text:
==**Surrendering to an enemy after being reduced to half Hit Points or less is never a dishonorable act**==, and is often the wisest course for survival. Being captured is neither shameful nor the end of a career — capture at the hands of a scheming sorceress or a robber-knight is a classic feature of the genre, and both Arthur and Lancelot are taken several times in the stories.

Conversely, **extending the offer of capture to a defeated enemy is a chivalrous act**, and the promise of ransom motivates most knights to prefer capture to killing. **Capturing enemies is potentially lucrative.**

## Capture and the Oath of Parole

Typical capture happens **during a battle**. Captured knights are **disarmed and herded together under guard**; once the fighting is over, the captives must swear the **Oath of Parole** — an oath of submission guaranteeing they will **not attempt escape or act treacherously** toward their captor.

In exchange for the oath, **the captor must supply shelter and food appropriate to the captive's rank**. ==To do otherwise deserves a **Selfish** check.==

- Depending on the captive's trustworthiness, the captor **may return the captive's sword, armor and horses** as a token of honor, earning a **Generous** check.
- This is honorable but **neither necessary nor often prudent** — the captive's arms and horses **belong to the captor by right of conquest**. ==A Player-knight does **not** take a Selfish check for keeping his captive's gear.==

## Raising the ransom

The captor allows the captive to **send word to his liege and family**, who then collect the funds — some from the peasants of the knight's holding, some from his family, some from his liege.

**What the liege contributes signals how much the captive is valued.** A favorite is assured of release, his lord paying the full amount if need be; **a troublesome or poor knight may get only a couple of libra.** A family has a duty to secure release and will pay whatever it must. A vassal knight can simply squeeze his peasants for the sum.

**Money rarely changes hands.** Ransoms are more often paid in **horses, fine cloth and expensive household wares** — tapestries, utensils, furniture — borne in carts to the captor's home. Raising the funds may take a long time; **the captive must be freed when payment is made.**

**Release on oath.** A captive may be **freed to collect his own ransom**, swearing an oath to return within a set time — ==**typically a year and a day**== — with or without the money.

## If the ransom is never paid

The captive **must serve as a loyal follower of his captor**, in borrowed armor, weapons and horse. The captor sets the length of service, but it must be enough to discharge the debt: **calculate the years required by comparing the difference in the Standard of Living at which he is kept.** A knight in such captivity would be wise to **seek loot and captives of his own** to hasten repayment.

## Scenario hooks

- The captive knight is released to collect his own ransom — **and does not return.**
- The captive **behaves treacherously while under the Oath of Parole.**
- **Nobody offers to pay** the captive's ransom, and the captor is stuck with him.
- The captor **demands an unusually large ransom**, far more than the captive is worth.

title: Feasting (Feasts & Banquets event)
text:
Feasts are major social set-pieces, treated on par with tournaments as a vehicle for interactions, schemes, rivalries, and alliances. A "feast" may be a holy/market day, a wedding or knighting, or just the meal itself. Play runs as a series of abstract **Feast Rounds**, each resolved around **Geniality** and **Feast Events**.

## Geniality

**Geniality** is a modifier measuring one's nobility in peers' eyes. Add it to **APP** and most **Courtly Skills** (Compose, Courtesy, Dancing, Fashion, Flirting, Gaming, Intrigue, Orate, Play Instrument, Singing) at court or during a feast. It also modifies **everyone else's Recognize** roll made about that knight in a courtly setting.

- Starting Geniality is set by the knight's **clothing** (based on Standard of Living + Fashion skill if applied). Lords maintain their knights at **Ordinary** level by default.
- **Geniality can never exceed the character's APP.**

**Clothing → Geniality (Table 3.1, Class Minimum column):**

| Class minimum | Clothing cost | Geniality |
|---|---|---|
| (a few denarii) | few d. | −5 |
| Mercenary Knight (no squire) | 120 d. | −3 |
| Mercenary Knight | £1 | +1 |
| Household / Vassal Knight | £2 | +2 |
| Estate Holder | £4 | +3 |
| Banneret | £8 | +4 |
| Baron | £16 | +5 |
| Rich Baron | £32 | +6 |
| Count, Duke, Minor King | — | — |

Knights may always dress **above** their station if they can afford it; the Class Minimum is the floor for that rank.

## Feast Rounds

Each Round ≈ 1–2 hours of eating, mixing, revelry, and private talk. The GM sets the number of Rounds up front by feast size (**Table 3.2**, suggested minimums):

| Size | Example | Min. Rounds |
|---|---|---|
| Small | A vassal knight's wedding | 2 |
| Medium | A neighborhood tournament's closing feast | 3 |
| Large | Easter feast for a duke | 4 |
| Royal | Arthur's Pentecost feast | 5 |

## Seating — "the Salt"

Where one sits speaks volumes — the seating at a feast or daily meal displays the whole relationship between a lord and his household, and sitting closer to the lord is a sign of status. Seating is by **rank first, then Glory** (all mercenary knights together, then all household knights, then all vassal knights, and so on); special circumstances can promote a character but **never** by random roll. **Newly made knights sit farthest from the high table** — though at the front of that area. Four areas, relative to the salt cellar at the high table (per-Round Geniality effect):

- **Above the Salt** (high table): **+2 Geniality/Round**, but **all Geniality losses from Events are doubled** ("all eyes on you").
- **Closer to the Salt** (lower table, near its head): **+1 Geniality/Round**.
- **Farther from the Salt** (default for most guests): no modifier.
- **On the Floor** (squires, dogs, snubbed guests): **−1 Geniality/Round**, or **−2/Round** if seated here through a fumbled Glory roll.

### The dapifer — who seats everyone

**The house *dapifer* ("meat server") is the officer responsible for seating everyone**, and it is the dapifer who guides each guest to their place.

- Being guided to **a different seat closer to the high table** is ==**"a sign of favor, but not a Favor"**== — everyone formerly ahead of the honoree **moves down a seat**.
- ==**Being told to sit lower than before is a serious insult.**== Telling a knight to sit **among the squires** is worse; telling a knight to sit **among the commoners** is an insult **worthy of them breaking with their lord**.

**Who else is in the hall:** if other high-ranking lords attend, **the women of the high table eat in the solar with the hostess**. At a large feast with visitors, **commoners eat elsewhere**; if enough knights come, **the squires give up their usual place and serve their knights at table** instead. Those On the Floor — squires, dogs, and deliberately snubbed guests — find a place to eat somewhere else in the hall, on fresh rushes or straw if the lord has put any down.

### The Glory Roll (seating placement)
Before the feast each knight makes one **unopposed Glory roll** (vs. Glory ÷ 1000). Feast size shifts the result: **small feast → move up one level of success; royal feast → move down one level** (no worse than Farther from the Salt unless fumbled).

**Table 3.3 — Feast Seating:**

| Result | Seating |
|---|---|
| Critical | Above the Salt |
| Success | Closer to the Salt |
| Failure | Farther from the Salt |
| Fumble | Re-roll Glory (this time a fumble counts as a simple failure), then take a seat **one position further down** than the re-roll gives. If that lands on Farther from the Salt, you **eat on the floor** with the dogs and squires. |

### Effects on Honor
A knight involuntarily seated **below** a same-rank knight who has **fewer Glory** must pass a **Modest** test or lose **1 Honor**. Fumbling the Glory roll — or having a **Famous/Exalted Proud** value — inflicts that 1 Honor loss automatically.

### Ceding your position
A character may **voluntarily** cede to a lower area (to sit with comrades) via a **Modest** test: success → check Modest and **gain 10 Glory** (**20** on a critical), then move down; failure → the move can't be arranged; fumble → it reads as disingenuous, costing **1 Honor**. Characters with Famous/Exalted Proud **may not** cede.

## Feast Events (cards)

Each Round, each knight totals **APP + Geniality + a Glory prominence bonus** (Table 3.4). That **Total APP** sets how many Feast Event Cards may be drawn (Table 3.5).

**Table 3.4 — Glory Prominence Modifier:**

| Glory | Title | Modifier |
|---|---|---|
| 0–999 | Non-knight | +0 |
| 1,000–2,999 | Unproven | +1 |
| 3,000–3,999 | Veteran | +2 |
| 4,000–5,999 | Respected | +3 |
| 6,000–7,999 | Notable | +4 |
| 8,000–11,999 | Renowned | +5 |
| 12,000–15,999 | Illustrious | +6 |
| 16,000–31,999 | Extraordinary | +7 |
| 32,000+ | Legendary | +8 |

| 4− | 0 |
| 5–9 | 1 |
| 10–14 | 2 |
| 15–19 | 3 |

| 30+ | 6 |

**Drawing rules:**
- Draw **one card at a time**, then either play it or draw again up to the Total APP limit. **The last card must always be played**, even if harmful.
- Total APP can rise mid-feast (from Geniality gains), unlocking more draws.
- A **Host Event Card** (goblet symbol) must be **played immediately** and ends drawing for that Round.
- Unplayed cards are reshuffled; played cards are set aside until the deck is exhausted, then reshuffled in.

**Reading a card:** most call for an opposed/unopposed Statistic roll — follow the card and apply results at once. Some cards are kept across Rounds for a bonus; some trigger rolls from every other attendee (each resolves individually). The **number at the bottom is the Geniality modifier** gained on playing the card, applied regardless of the card's other dice results; your Geniality changes only when the card is put in play.

### Other Events (no card)
A knight who won't risk a card instead picks one of four activities — **Gossiping, flirting, gaming, or eating/drinking** — and rolls unopposed vs. the relevant Skill/Trait (**Flirting, Gaming, Intrigue, or Indulgent**), modified by Geniality. **Success** → a check to that Skill/Trait; **critical** → also earn **Glory equal to Total APP**. Use **Table 3.6: Random Feast Courses** (1D20 per course, three courses) to generate a "favorite dish" or add colour.

## Departing the Feast

**Failing to attend at all** when invited is a grave insult — attend for at least one Round or risk dire consequences. After the first Round, a knight may retire by **begging leave** with a **Courtesy** roll:
- **Success:** a check; **critical:** also **+10 Glory**. Host is gratified.
- **Failure:** dismissed curtly; **lose 1D3 Geniality** (min 0).
- **Fumble:** left without leave / gave offence; **lose 1 Honor and all accumulated Geniality**.

**Forced Departure:** some Event Cards drag a knight out early (passing out drunk, napping after excess, leaving with a lover). These need **no Courtesy roll**, but others notice and it may still cost Honor at the GM's discretion.

## Feasting Glory (end of feast)

At the last Round, total the **Geniality gained solely from Feast Events** (exclude starting Geniality) and compare to **Table 3.7**:

- **Below threshold:** Glory = (**Appeal + Geniality**) × **Rounds attended**, **max 100 Glory**.
- **Meets/exceeds threshold:** that Glory **plus the bonus** (standout guest). If several beat it, the **highest accumulated Geniality** wins the bonus; ties go to **highest Glory**.

**Table 3.7 — Geniality Threshold:**

| Size | Threshold | Bonus Glory |
|---|---|---|
| Small | 5 | +10 |
| Medium | 7 | +25 |
| Large | 9 | +50 |
| Royal | 11 | +100 |

*Example: at a medium feast Sir Avalloc (APP 11) accrues 6 Geniality → (11+6)×3 = **51 Glory**. With 8 Geniality (beating the threshold of 7) → 51 + 25 = **76 Glory** as the standout guest.*
