title: Fine Amor (Romance) — Adoration, Glory in the Beloved's Name & Consummation
text:
**Fine amor**, or Romance, is the **chaste adulation of a lover to obtain Inspiration** — originally codified by Queen Guenever. It begins when a knight becomes infatuated with a lady or courtier, consumed by a **chaste** desire to win their favor and inspired to great deeds. The knight must think of them constantly, seek their attention, and **jealously protect their honor**.

==To gain the **Passive Glory** for the romance, the knight must have an **Adoration (Person)** Passion and fulfil the other requirements of the **Romantic Knight** ideal.==

## Increasing the Beloved's opinion

A knight raises his standing with the Beloved by **giving gifts**, **doing favors**, or **succeeding at tasks they have requested**. The Beloved may **demand a task as proof of affection**.

## Glory in the Beloved's name

**The Beloved may earn Glory for deeds done in their name.**

- ==If a knight defeats an enemy — in mortal combat **or at a tournament** — and **sends them to the Beloved** with word that they were overcome in the Beloved's name, **the Beloved earns the same Combat Glory award** as if they had defeated the enemy personally.==
- The knight may also **donate other Glory awards** earned while inspired by the Adoration (Person) Passion:
  - **Donating 10 Glory** earns a **check to Adoration**.
  - **Donating 100 Glory** automatically **raises Adoration by one point**.
  - **No more than one Adoration point per year** may be gained this way.
  - Donations must be made **at the time of the award** and come from a **single award** — they **may not be banked or combined**.

## Consummation

**Fine amor is a spiritual practice.** ==Physical consummation **annihilates the Amor**.== The **Adoration** Passion is **removed and replaced by Love at half its value** — **Love (Spouse)** if the couple marry, **Love (Person)** if not.

The Lover and Beloved may go on practising Romance, but the reward is diminished: **the knight may no longer grant his own Glory awards to his lover**, though he **may still capture knights in their name**, earning them Glory that way.

> **Period note.** From the **Romance Period** onward, fine amor is codified into **Courtly Love** and the process of adoration and seduction becomes a ritualized social dance — a more detailed method of wooing covered in other Pendragon supplements.

title: Hunting — the Chase Procedure (Tables 3.8, 3.9 & 3.10)
text:
The **Hunting** Skill covers everything in the noble chase except Weapon Skills: what the blasts of the horn mean; whether a beast is one of **chase, venery, or vermin** (field — buck, doe, fox, marten, roe; forest — hart, hind, hare, boar, wolf; lesser — badger, wild cat, otter); care of hounds and their cries; identifying spoor and tracking from it; the best way to kill each animal; and **breaking** — butchering and field-dressing so that everyone from hounds and dog boys to the sponsor gets their correct share.

A hunt **requires dogs and horses**, and is enhanced by **bush beaters** and a **forester** as guide. The rules below assume all of these.

**Armor.** Knights hunt in a **gambeson (4 points)** or **aketon (2 points)**, not full harness. ==Knights in **mail or plate** suffer **−5 to Hunting**, and impose the same −5 on everyone else in their party== — the clanking is audible for a long way.

**Avoidance** is the animal's Statistic for running, hiding and deceiving pursuers. Values are in Chapter 8: Bestiary, p. 173.

## Sequence of a hunt

**1 · The Harboring.** The party selects ("harbors") the quarry. Professional huntsmen gather **tokens** from various beasts — tufts of fur, spoor, pieces of antler, dragon scales — and present them at the **Gathering**, a combined social event and planning session over breakfast in the field. ==The **host**, or the guest with the **most Glory**, chooses which quarry to hunt.==

**Hunting Rounds last about an hour.** A day allows **6 Rounds in winter, 8 in spring and autumn, 10 in summer.** When they are used up, the hunt ends and everyone returns to their lodgings.

The party chooses a **leader** — the character with the highest Hunting Skill. They may **split into several parties** to get more Hunting rolls.

**2 · The Unharboring — setting the track.** Draw **four parallel lines numbered 1–4**, and place the quarry's marker **ahead of position #1**. Every participant gets a marker; leaders and followers are set by their relative positions.

Placement is by **Hunting Skill** and **Movement Rate**:

- Every leader makes an **unopposed Hunting roll**: **critical → #1**, **success → #2**, **failure → #3**, **fumble → #4**. Followers are placed with their leader automatically.
- Then each participant rolls against **their horse's Movement Rate**: **critical** moves the marker **forward one**, **success** stays put, **failure** moves **back one**, **fumble** moves **back two**.

**3 · The Pursuit.** Repeat each Hunting Round until the prey is found (the Abay) or the day ends. ==A marker that ever drops **behind position #4** has fallen too far behind and may not take further part in the hunt.==

Each leader makes an **opposed roll of Hunting against the prey's Avoidance** on Table 3.8. Obstacles are resolved individually by each character, and **must be navigated before advancing**.

### Table 3.8 — Hunting vs Avoidance Results

| Hunter's result | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Critical success** | Encounter an obstacle and **advance two positions** |
| **Win** | Encounter an obstacle and **advance one position** |
| **Partial success or tie** | Encounter an obstacle |
| **Lose** | Move back one position |
| **Fumble** | Move back two positions |

### Table 3.9 — Hunting Obstacles (2D6)

**Only one roll on this table is made per hunting party**, but **each knight tests the indicated Statistic individually**. A failed roll costs **one position from the indicated advance** — possibly separating you from the party, unless everyone slows to let you catch up.

| 2D6 | Obstacle |
|---:|---|
| **2** | Hidden ditch or sudden precipice. Roll the **horse's DEX** to avoid a fall doing **2D6 to both horse and rider**. |
| **3** | Dangerous branches or outcropping rocks. **Horse's DEX** to avoid a fall and **1D6**. |
| **4–5** | A small stream or ditch. **Horsemanship** to jump it. Failure = the horse refused; **fumble** = rider and horse both fall for **1D6**. |
| **6** | Birds flush underfoot. **Horsemanship** to avoid a fall for **1D6**. |
| **7** | Confusing tracks. **Hunting** roll, or lose the prey and **move back one position**. |
| **8** | A fallen tree leaves only a small passage. **Hunting** to find a way through, or **back one position**. |
| **9** | Thorny bramble bushes. The **horse** must make a **CON** roll or take **1D6**. |
| **10** | Hunting horns or barking dogs in the distance. **Awareness** to follow the sound — success ==**moves you to the quarry's position**==. |
| **11** | A dead end. **Awareness**. On a failure, roll **twice more** on this table (ignoring further 11s) and apply both. |
| **12** | ==**The prey comes charging back!** Advance to the Abay.== |

**4 · The Abay.** Once one or more knights catch up with the prey's token, the hunters must drive the animal until it can go no further and turns at bay. Horns sound to call in lost dogs, reckless gallopers and winded hangers-on, all converging for the kill.

- The **first character on the scene** — or the one with the **highest Glory** — may make **one free attack**; alternatively they may hold near the creature until reinforcements arrive and fight it in normal melee.
- ==**Tradition reserves the first blow for the host or honored guest.**== Anyone unwilling to wait rolls **Modest/Proud**; if **Modest succeeds and they strike anyway, they lose 1 Honor**.
- If several want the first attack, the **highest Movement Rate** takes it (ties broken by **DEX**).
- The first attack is an **opposed roll: the hunter's Weapon Skill against the prey's Avoidance**, on Table 3.10.

### Table 3.10 — Weapon vs Avoidance Results

| Weapon vs Avoidance | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Critical success** | Inflict normal Damage **+4D6**. The prey turns angrily and **begins fighting next Round**, if still conscious. |
| **Win** | Inflict normal damage. The prey fights next Round **unless badly hurt**, in which case it Avoids again. |
| **Partial success or tie** | The prey escapes; everyone at the Abay returns to **position #4**. Roll Hunting next segment at **+5**. |
| **Lose** | The prey escapes; everyone at the Abay returns to **position #4**. |
| **Fumble** | The prey escapes; everyone returns to **#4**, and the Player-knight **falls for 1D6** trying to reach it. |

**5 · The Rush.** If the quarry lives after the first attack, **as many as three characters with melee weapons** may attack while the beast tries to escape or to close.

- **If it flees:** it still uses its **Avoidance** on Table 3.10 to oppose these attacks rather than a Combat Skill. With several attackers it takes penalties to Avoidance exactly as it would to a Combat Skill against multiple opponents.
- **If it fights:** use its **Combat Skills** as normal.

**6 · Normal Combat.** If the creature survives the Rush, the hunt becomes ordinary melee. If instead it flees, ==the hunt resumes and returns to the Pursuit.==

title: Intoxication (Tables 3.11 & 3.12) — Getting Drunk, Staying Drunk & the Hangover
text:
Alcohol flows freely in Arthur's Britain. **Ale** is the commonest — village alewives brew it from malted barley with herbs like clover and heather, and sell it from their dwellings (*alehouses*). **Beer** is ale flavoured with hops. **Mead** is fermented honey, spices and herbs, preferred among the less Romanized Cymric nobility. **Wine** is preferred in the cities and among the Roman clergy, imported in quantity from the continent. **Hard liquor has not yet been discovered.**

Common ale is **"small ale"** — watery and weak, and hard to get drunk on. Wealthier lords keep professional brew masters making stronger ales spiced with imported cinnamon and ginger, and serve copious mead and **unmixed** wine. This accounts for much of the outrageous behaviour of guests used to weaker brew, who get roaring drunk on an equal volume of the stronger stuff.

Severity is set by an **Indulgent** roll; the state is then **maintained by an Energetic roll** once every two hours.

## Table 3.11 — Intoxication Results (unopposed **Indulgent**)

| Indulgent result | State of Intoxication | Modifiers |
|---|---|---|
| **Critical** | **Roaring Drunk** | **+10** to Lustful, Reckless, Indulgent and Valorous; **−10 to all Skills** |
| **Success** | **Drunk** | **+5** to Flirting, Orate, Lustful, Reckless, Indulgent and Valorous; **−5** to all other Skills |
| **Failure** | Sober | No modifiers |
| **Fumble** | Sober | **No Indulgent rolls need be made for the remainder of the scene** |

**A critical is the worst outcome on this table**, and a fumble removes the character from the drinking entirely.

**Modifiers to Indulgent:**

- **Mead:** +2
- **Wine:** +5 (or higher for exotic wines)
- **Feasting in the presence of enemies:** −5
- **Attending a royal feast:** −2

**No experience checks while drunk.** A character who is intoxicated has impaired awareness of their own actions and so cannot learn from them — **they gain no experience checks to their Skills.**

## Table 3.12 — Intoxicated Activity Level (unopposed **Energetic**)

Intoxication lasts **as long as the drinker is awake**. Roll **Energetic for every two hours of game time — equal to one Feast Round** — until everyone retires.

| Energetic result | State | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Critical** | **Sobered up** | No modifiers; the character's state is now **Sober** |
| **Success** | Dull and sleepy | **−5** to all Skills |
| **Failure** | **Passed out** | No activity; if woken, **−10** to all Skills |
| **Fumble** | **Comatose** | **Will not awake under any circumstances until the next morning** |

**Always keep the worst result of the previous rolls**, and the penalties from this roll are **added to** any arising from the character's intoxication level.

**Modifiers to Energetic:**

- **Roaring Drunk:** −10
- **Drunk:** −5
- **Debilitated:** −5

## The hangover

Characters who **lose consciousness** must roll **CON the next day at −5** (**−10 if comatose**). **Failure indicates a hangover: −5 to all Skills for the remainder of the day.**

## Where this is invoked

The **drink cards** in the Feast Event deck ("More Drink", "Mead", "Raucous Contest", "Tipsy", "Overindulgence", and the rest) all defer to these rules — see [[gm.arthurian-acts.feasting]]. Note that **Temperate/Indulgent** decisions on those cards come first; this table resolves what the drinking then does.

title: Races and Chases — the Line Track
text:
Races and chases run on **the same positional track as the hunt**. Draw a series of parallel lines, or mark areas on a map, and place tokens for each party. ==Use **no fewer than four lines**.==

- **In a race**, everyone starts on the same line.
- **In a chase**, the pursued may have a **head start of one or two lines**, depending on the circumstances that began it.

## The Chase Round

Everyone makes an **unopposed roll against their Movement Rate** — or their **steed's**, if mounted:

| Result | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Critical** | Advance **two lines** |
| **Success** | Advance **one line** |
| **Failure** | No advancement |
| **Fumble** | Roll **DEX** (or **Horsemanship** if mounted) — see below |

**On a fumble:** a **failed** DEX/Horsemanship roll means the character has ==**come up lame or winded and may not continue**== (with appropriate consequences if being chased); a **successful** roll means an obstacle merely delays them — roll on **Table 3.9: Hunting Obstacles** if appropriate, or simply have them **miss the next round of rolls**.

**Allied characters on the same line** are treated as **one group**, for simplicity.

## When pursuer and pursued meet

Each time a Chase Round ends with **a pursuer and the pursued on the same line**, they make an **opposed roll based on the Player-knight's stated intention**:

- **Standing and fighting:** Weapon Skill vs Weapon Skill.
- **Losing the trail** in an overland chase by cutting through rough terrain: **opposed Hunting** rolls.
- **Simply speeding away:** treat it as an **Evade** action — the character's **Movement Rate against the pursuer's Weapon Skill**.

**If the pursued wins:** they inflict damage if using a Weapon Skill, and **advance one line**. **If the pursuer wins:** they may inflict damage and have ==**cornered their quarry**, who must either fight a full combat or surrender==.

**Pursuers can catch up more than once** over a chase.

## Ending it

- **A race** is won by the first to reach the final line — but **resolve everyone's Movement Rate rolls before declaring a winner**. On a tie, everyone at the finish makes **opposed DEX (or Horsemanship)** rolls to see who crossed first.
- **A chase** ends when the pursued **reaches the final line and escapes** — getting away from any pursuers who reach it too.

title: Seducing Someone at Court — Commoners, Nobles, Adultery & Discovery
text:
A potentially dangerous act, **whatever the stations of those involved** — discretion is advised.

## Seducing a commoner

A successful **Flirting** roll, which triggers an **opposed Chaste/Lustful** roll.

The GM may apply **negative modifiers to Flirting** — the commoner is happily married or in love with someone else, the Player-knight has **low APP**, or has previously failed important Courtly Skill rolls such as Dancing. Conversely, **high APP or significant Glory** may earn a **bonus**.

## Seducing a noblewoman or courtier

Social equals, raised in an atmosphere that **continually warns against smooth-talking, insincere visitors**. A **Christian** court is likely to emphasize and honor chastity; even in a **Pagan** court, public wantonness may be frowned upon depending on the time of year. **It requires much effort.**

- ==**The Player-knight must first perform a Favor** for them, of a value depending on their rank and status== — valuable gifts, deeds, or dangerous actions.
- ==The GM **secretly sets a minimum threshold** for how many Favors will convince them.==
- **Secrecy is absolutely required** for the safety and reputation of everyone involved.

## Consequences and discovery

**If a liaison between a man and a woman is discovered**, the GM is free to **roll for childbirth in the Winter Phase** to see whether the union was productive.

**With a common servant**, depending on the disposition of the lord or lady, **the servant may be beaten or lose their position**. The Player-knight's reputation usually suffers only slightly — but **greatly** if the court particularly upholds Christian morality, or if the servant was the lord or lady's personal favorite, whatever their religion. ==**Honor loss is ensured if the seduction appears in any way non-consensual.**==

## Adultery

**Blatantly dangerous and illegal.** Adultery is sex with someone outside a marriage — a **legally binding contract** tied to property and inheritance rights. Canon Law does not discriminate between men and women, but **custom weighs heavily in favor of the husband**: a man whose wife has committed adultery is **cuckolded**, and lives in fear that any child she bears in the next year is not of his blood.

Being cuckolded is a **serious dishonor requiring revenge**:

- Catching wife and lover **in flagrante delicto**, the husband has the ==**legal right to kill the cuckolder**==. If **Merciful**, he may merely **castrate** him.
- **Either act restores the Honor lost** to the cuckolding.
- He may **send his wife to a nunnery**, or keep her to perform her duties as steward — but little more.

> **This is the state of things at the start of the campaign.** As the Arthurian ethos evolves, many nobles develop a more forgiving understanding of seduction and being seduced.

title: The Grand Melee & the Joust — Long-Form Procedures (Tables 3.16 & 3.17)
text:
## The Grand Melee

A **mock battle** over a field of several square miles with vague boundaries, between the two villages where the teams are lodged. At either end a **recet** is marked out — the team's rear area, banked and guarded by armed footmen who keep opposing knights out.

A melee may last **half a day** for a neighborhood tournament, or **several days** for regional and royal ones, with contestants dwindling as they are captured or wounded.

Contestants divide into two even sides, **charge with lances at the signal**, and fall into melee once the lances break. Teams are divided into **conroi**-like groups that support each other and **share loot and ransom costs**. ==A captive may be **rescued by friends before he is brought into the recet**.== In the Boy King Period knights are aided by **squires and kippers**, whose job is to lead or drag captives off the field into the recet — a practice that **ends during the Conquest Period**. During the day knights may **retire to their recet** for first aid, rest, a drink or a snack, but will rush back if their side is losing.

### Procedure

==**A tournament melee is run with the full rules of Chapter 6: Battle**, because that is exactly what it is.== Player-knights choose a team and a **conroi leader** before it begins.

- The GM assembles **Encounters and Opportunities appropriate to a tournament** — knights exclusively.
- **Melee size corresponds to regular battle sizes, but ==Intensity is only half==.**
- Participation Glory comes from **Table 6.6: Battle Participation Glory**, by melee size.
- Individual Glory for defeating opponents is awarded as always — but ==**with rebated weapons, award only one-tenth the normal Glory**==.

**The Grand Prize** goes to whoever the judges — tracking deeds of prowess through the heralds — decide was the most valiant, dashing and effective.

### The rules of the melee, in full

- **Lances and sharp weapons are rebated.**
- **A knight is defeated when unhorsed, knocked unconscious, killed (accidentally, of course), or on surrendering.**
- When an opponent is defeated, ==**their steed may be taken**== and becomes the winner's prize **if the knight or his squire can bring it to the safe area and leave it there**.
- Knights on the same team, and especially the same conroi, **are expected to assist each other**.
- **Multiple opponents may attack a single knight.**

## The Joust

Formal jousting events take about **ten years into Arthur's reign** to appear, growing from ostentatious challenges by prideful show-offs into formalized elimination contests. They are often placed **before** the melee — still the main event — so that as many knights as possible can take part, since the melee often removes a contestant entirely. Each contestant **draws a random opponent** and meets him for **up to three passes** on a ground called the **list**.

### Procedure

A series of **one-on-one contests using opposed Charge Skills**; each roll is a **pass**. The intention is **not to kill** but to unhorse the opponent humiliatingly, or failing that to be **first to break three lances** on his shield. Jousting lances are specially built to break more often.

==**Tournament jousting uses Table 3.16, not the normal Mounted Charge results**== — the Charge Skill is still used, but the outcomes differ. **Unrebated** joust events, held by bloodthirsty knights, use the **normal Mounted Charge procedure** instead.

### Table 3.16 — Joust Results (opposed Charge)

| Opposed Charge roll | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Critical** | **Perfect hit.** Automatically knocks the opponent from the saddle (**no DEX roll**) for **2D6** falling damage; on a failed **Horsemanship** roll he is **crushed under his horse** (takes the horse's Charge Damage). Lance breaks. |
| **Win** | Hit and break lance; opponent makes a **DEX** roll to remain seated. |
| **Tie, double critical** | Lance to lance, **both lances break**; both make **Horsemanship** rolls to prevent horse knockdown. |
| **Tie, double success** | Both hit, both lances break, both make **DEX** to stay seated. |
| **Tie, double failure** | Both miss, no lances break. |
| **Tie, double fumble** | **1D6:** 1–2 both strike the opponent's horse (**both disqualified**) · 3–4 both miss and the **horses collide** if there is no tilt, each taking the other's full **Charge Damage** (with a tilt, treat as 5–6) · 5–6 both miss but **fall from their horses untouched** for **1D6** each. |
| **Partial success** | Hit; **lance breaks if the Charge roll was an odd number**. |
| **Loss** | Miss; **DEX** roll to remain seated or take **1D6** falling damage. |
| **Fumble** | **1D20:** 1–5 hit the tilt (no tilt → treat as 6–10) · 6–10 **hit the opponent's horse — disqualified** · 11–12 **dropped the lance** before striking, looking like an incompetent youth (**−5 to Courtly Skills for the rest of the tournament**) · 13–14 thrown, horse runs off, **1D6** · 15–16 hit his saddle, possibly angering him (**Forgiving** roll) · 17–18 fall off, **1D6** · 19–20 ==fall with a **foot caught in the stirrup and are dragged for 3D6, no armor protection**==. |

### Joust Glory

- **Winning a round: one-tenth the opponent's Combat Glory.**
- **With unrebated lances: half Combat Glory.**

### Joust scoring *(introduced in the Tournament Period)*

A formal points system for strikes to the chest, helmet or shield. **Three passes** is the commonest encounter; the knight with the most points wins and advances. Some tournaments skip elimination entirely and take the **highest score at the end**.

- **Unhorsing:** 3 points, **or immediate victory**, depending on the rules in force
- **Lance to lance:** 2 points
- **Broken lance:** 1 point
- **Hit but lance not broken:** 0 points, but used as the **tie-breaker**

## Later-Period customs

- A **tilt** — a barrier down the centre of the list — is raised in the Tournament Period to stop the horses colliding, with new lances and armor for safety.
- **Display of the helms:** the day before, all knights lay out helmets and shields in a row to be identified. Judges and ladies scrutinize them and **point out anyone dishonorable, in exile, or otherwise unfit**; if the accusations prove true, ==**the contestant is ejected from the competition**==.
- A **Vespers Tourney** on the evening before the main event lets new knights compete.
- By mid-Tournament Period **the melee is dropped entirely**; individual talent and pomp outweigh martial prowess, entry fees rise steeply, and participants must prove **three generations of knighthood**.

## Tournament Prizes — Table 3.17 (1D20 + size modifier)

Prizes are **not usually coin** but something fancy worth the indicated value. **Tournament Size Roll Modifier:** Neighborhood **+0** · Local **+1** · Regional Small **+2** · Regional Large **+3** · Regal **+4** · Regal Grand **+5**.

| Roll | Prize |
|---:|---|
| 1 | Gold belt, £1 |
| 2 | Gold ring, £1 |
| 3 | Advanced nasal helm, gold trimmed, crested with a silver figure of Saint Bartholomew, £2 |
| 4 | Advanced hauberk, £2 |
| 5 | Garnished arming sword, £3 |
| 6 | Gold chain, £3 |
| 7 | Advanced hauberk, £3 |
| 8 | White scent or gaze hound with a gold collar, £3 |
| 9 | Superbly wrought advanced nasal helm, elaborately crested (**Armor Protection 3**), £5 |
| 10 | Gold circlet or crown, £5 |
| 11 | Rich knight's clothing, £5 |
| 12 | Big ruby, £6 |
| 13 | Advanced nasal helm, diamond trimmed, crested with a gold naked Cupid tied to a laurel tree, £7 |
| 14 | Mid-sized diamond, £7 |
| 15 | Gold ring with a big ruby, £7 |
| 16 | Gold ring with a mid-sized diamond, £8 |
| 17 | Exquisite gold figurine of a lion, vulture, or other kingly beast, £9 |
| 18 | Superlative knight's clothing, £10 |
| 19 | Gold clasp or brooch decorated with little rubies, £11 |
| 20 | Gold rod or baton mounted with a big ruby, £11 |
| 25 | Noble grey courser, £27 (**Normal Courser stats, but Movement 22**) |

*The table continues past 20 for larger tournaments; entries are drawn from recorded twelfth- to sixteenth-century tournament prizes. Invent comparable prizes and use the table as a value guide.*

title: Tournaments — Entry, Sizes & the Short-Form Resolution (Tables 3.12–3.15)
text:
Tournaments — originally **hastiludes** ("spear play") — are sporting events where knights with blunted weapons try to unhorse each other. Events use **"arms of peace"**: rebated weapons and lances built to break easily.

**Jousts are open only to tried warriors** who know how to ride armored and how to fall when hit. A competition may be restricted to nobles of rank, to knights who can prove **three generations of knightly ancestors**, or to those who can afford a steep entry fee. Prizes and Glory await the victors; **humiliation and the loss of a prized horse or armor** await the losers.

Announced **months in advance**; knights arrive a week to a day early, lodging in the **two villages that bound the melee field** — ==which village you lodge in determines which melee team you are on== — or in pavilions near the grounds. A **bohort** may be held where squires practise and show off against their peers.

## Entering

- **Only knights may enter.** Vassal, household or mercenary makes no difference. **Squires and cavalry** may take part only in their own special events.
- **Knights without honor or of ill repute may not participate.**
- ==**Participation in disguise is allowed.**==
- **A fee is required.**

## Short-Form Tournaments

For a tourney with no unusual events planned — a handful of rolls, fast enough to resolve in passing while the knights are on adventure.

**1 · Tournament Difficulty Level (TDL).** ==Equal to the **worst Charge Skill among the Player-knights**==, then modified by Table 3.14.

**2 · Size.** Roll on **Table 3.12: Master Tournament Table**, which also fixes Participant and Champion's Glory and the prize. **Add +5** in the Tournament or Grail Quest Periods, **+10** in the Twilight Period.

**3 · Resolve.** Make an **opposed roll against the TDL** — a **Weapon Skill** of choice for the Melee, **Charge** for the Joust — on Table 3.15. Then make a **second opposed roll on the same table for accumulated damage**. ==It is therefore possible to **win the event and still be grievously wounded**.== A knight who competes in one event and stays healthy enough for the other may do both, **doubling the potential Glory**.

**Courtly Rolls** (Table 3.12) are rolled **even under the short form**.

### Table 3.12 — Master Tournament Table

| 1D20 | Size | Attending knights | Participant Glory | Champion's Glory | Prize | Days | Joust rounds | Courtly rolls | Cost to sponsor | Barber's Skill |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|---|---:|
| 1–15 | Neighborhood | 25–50 | 15 | 20 | £1–2 | 2 | 6 | 1D3 | £6 | 14 |
| 16–18 | Local | 100–150 | 25 | 35 | £4–6 | 2–3 | 7 | 1D6 | £24–40 | 14 |
| 19–20 | Regional, Small | 200–300 | 50 | 75 | £8–12 | 4–5 | 8 | 1D6 | £60–90 | 17 |
| 19–20 | Regional, Large | 400–600 | 75 | 150 | £16–24 | 6–7 | 9 | 1D6+1 | £140–220 | 18 |
| 19–20 | Regal | 800–1,600 | 100 | 350 | £32–64 | 8–12 | 10 | 1D6+3 | £330–800 | 19 |
| 19–20 | Regal, Grand | 2,400 | 150 | 500 | £96 | 14 | 11 | 2D6+4 | £1,300 | 20 |

- **Joust Rounds** — the elimination rounds needed to reach a winner, if not using the short form.
- **Courtly Rolls** — how many Courtly Skills each Player-knight may roll for checks.
- **Cost to Sponsor** — ==only King Arthur can afford a Grand Regal tournament, and only three are held in his reign.==
- **Barber's Skill** — unless seen to by a wife, lover, or their own entourage, seriously wounded knights are attended by a professional with this value in **both First Aid and Chirurgery**.

### Table 3.13 — Tournament Opponents (1D20 + Joust Round)

| Roll | Charge | Weapon\* | Damage | Armor | Horse damage | Horse armor |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|---:|
| 1–5 | 13 | 13 | 4D6 | 10 + 6 | 5D6 | 1 |
| 6–13 | 15 | 15 | 5D6 | 10 + 6 | 6D6 | 2 |
| 14–19 | 17 | 16 | 5D6 | 11 + 6 | 6D6 | 4 |
| 20+ | 19 | 18 | 5D6 | 12 + 6 | 6D6 | 4 |

\* Usually Sword, but may be One-Handed Hafted for a mace or axe. Adjust armor for the Period. **Assume DEX 12**, or roll **2D6+5**. *These opponents are for the Boy King Period only.*

### Table 3.14 — TDL Modifiers

| 1D20 | TDL modifier | Cause |
|---|---:|---|
| 1–3 | **−10** | Tournament is cursed or poorly attended |
| 4–8 | **−5** | Hot or wet weather |
| 9–13 | 0 | Nothing unusual |
| 14–15 | **+5** | Famous knight(s) or a family foe present |
| 16–18 | **+10** | Extraordinary knight(s) or a personal foe present |
| 19+ | **+15** | Round Table knight(s) or an Inspired enemy present |

### Table 3.15 — Short-Form Resolution

| Result | Glory award | Damage |
|---|---|---|
| **Critical** | **Champion's Glory** | No damage |
| **Win** | Participant Glory **×2** | 1D6 |
| **Tie** | Participant Glory **×1½** | 1D6 |
| **Partial success** | Participant Glory | 3D6 |
| **Loss** | Participant Glory | 4D6 |
| **Fumble** | Participant Glory **×½** | 5D6 |

==**Damage here is unaffected by armor**== — it represents small hurts accumulated through the tourney that penetrated the harness, and **may only be healed by Natural Healing**.

## The shape of the event

**The Invocation.** On the morning, the sponsor gives a speech; contestants parade before judges and onlookers. Heralds present the **Lady of the Tournament** — the sponsor's wife, or an available lady whose hand may be offered to the victor. The sponsor introduces the **Grand Marshall**, the **judges** (well-known veterans and important ladies) and the **heralds**, displays the prizes, and **states the terms of capture and the ransoms** to be enforced in the melee.

**Each day** ends with the judges naming the best fighter and awarding a prize, then a **feast** with music, dances, jongleurs, bards and troubadours late into the night.

**At the close**, event winners are named and given prizes, and the champion — the **knight of honor** (*chevalier d'honneur*) — is acclaimed. All combatants meet unarmed and unarmored in the lists to embrace and **prove no grudges are held**. Captives arrange to ransom back armor, horses, or their own bodies. A final feast is held; those too wounded to travel **remain as guests of their host**.

title: Visiting a Foreign Court — Patrols, the Gate, Hospitality, Diplomacy & Spying
text:
Any court not of your liege. A common event — escorting a travelling lord or lady, or riding on adventure. **Certain protocols are followed**, and both parties expect formal behaviour.

## 1 · Meeting a patrol

Meeting a border patrol will **certainly** happen shortly after crossing into another county or kingdom. **Courtesy** and **Recognize** carry the encounter:

- **Courtesy** success — a good impression, and relations are smoothed.
- **Recognize** success — learn something about the foreign knights: **their famous Skills and Combat Skills, and which lord they serve**, which is valuable information and opens the social convention of **flattery**.

**If expected:** the knights are welcomed and escorted to the lord's castle, a messenger riding ahead so the hall can be prepared.

**If not expected:** the patrol demands their business and expects them to announce their intentions. Make a peaceful gesture and state the business, or simply say you are "passing through". The patrol may let them pass — especially if their lords are friendly — or bring them in for questioning.

> [!danger] Refusing to answer
> ==Resistance creates hostilities.== If the knights refuse information, the GM may add a modifier to a **Suspicious** roll for the patrol; on a success the patrol **reads the refusal as a hostile act**. If the Player-knights are outnumbered they are **attacked**, with a squire or messenger galloping to the castle as combat is joined. The lord musters his household knights and hastens to the spot. ==**Fighting the local patrol makes enemies, and the lord need show no mercy to strangers.**==

## 2 · At the gate

A gate open to local traffic still has **guards checking identity and business**, especially of armed and mounted knights.

If the gate is closed: ride up, knock, **blow a horn, ring a bell, or shout** until the **porter** comes. ==Porter is a prestigious post — he decides who enters immediately and who waits.== A successful **Courtesy** roll helps an unexpected party; the porter may admit them at once, but is **more likely to send word to his lord** while the knights **wait outside the gate, however miserable the weather**.

Eventually a **castellan, steward or other official** welcomes them. **Hospitality must be extended by the lord's man and accepted by the visitors.**

## 3 · The courtyard and quarters

Grooms and stewards offer to take the steeds; **knights should order their own squires to see to the horses** with the grooms' help. Squires typically **remain in or near the stables until summoned the next day**, guarding horses and belongings — though a knight may use his squire as body servant and messenger. Food is brought to them and they **bed down in the hay**.

**Quarters** vary with Period and the lord's wealth: a furnished tower room shared between the knights, or **a pile of clean straw in the hall**. ==Whoever normally occupies that room or floor space **is moved out** to make room.== A separate **guest house**, where one exists, is reserved for important visitors — **a successful Courtesy roll can open its door even to the lowliest knight**.

**Washing:** ewers, buckets, soap and towels are brought. A leader of significant rank is offered **a bath**, and the other knights may use it after him — ==**the water is not usually changed**==.

## 4 · Being introduced

The knights are escorted to the reigning lord or lady, who may receive them in the high seat, **in their bed chamber**, or while otherwise occupied.

==**The Player-knight with the highest Glory should reply for everyone** and make a **Courtesy** roll, which sets the tone of the encounter.== The lord may ask their business or destination but is **not bound to** — the **old Cymric custom is to offer hospitality first**.

Once welcomed, the knights are **at the mercy of their host** and are usually invited to stay. The lord is **under no obligation to see them again**; a successful **Courtesy** roll may earn an invitation **to dine with the lord's family**, for which the knights are expected to wear **their absolute best clothing** — and impressive manners or a generous host may see them **loaned costly robes for the stay**.

## 5 · During the stay

**Limited leave of the castle**, always with a court servant as escort who **deftly steers them away from what the lord does not want seen**. If that servant is a commoner, a successful **Folklore** roll puts them at ease, and a successful **Intrigue** roll may learn something of the castle's goings-on.

**Dining.** Seats appropriate to station, **bumping the residents down** to make room; notable or renowned knights may be offered the **high table**, possibly beside the lord. Dinner talk is boasting, good humour and trivialities — run the **Feasting** procedure if desired. A lord holding to the **old Cymric tradition** asks their business **only after the final course**, often preceded or followed by a **request for news of the outside world** — an opportunity for **Orate** rolls.

**Entertainment.** The lord may be showing off, may enjoy their company, or ==may be offering distractions to **delay a purposeful meeting** for political reasons==. Evenings bring musicians, jugglers, pantomimists and fools; wealthy courts add poetry and a renowned bard. Many lords keep the ancient tradition of **"passing the harp"** at the end of a meal. Knights may offer, or be commanded, to perform — **Compose, Orate, Play (Instrument), Singing**. A **dance** allows **Dancing** rolls, endearing them to the court and to anyone they are Flirting with. **Games of chance** use **Gaming**; drinking contests are a perennial favourite. **Caroling** may carry an implicit wager — the least entertaining member, by consensus vote, **suffers a forfeit**, often specified in the carol.

## 6 · Departing — begging one's leave

==**Once given Hospitality, knights must not depart without the lord's permission.**== This is **begging one's leave**, and it is a vital part of Hospitality. ==**Departing without it costs a point of Hospitality.**==

When the time is right, the knights may be given **food for the road, directions, and a guide** for the next leg, and offered a **parting stirrup cup of wine**. If they are held in esteem, they may be **asked to bear messages or tidings to other courts**.

## Diplomacy at Court

The simple version: meet **privately** with the lord or lady — and their councillors, clerks and priests — and state your case.

- The opposing diplomat may be the lord, the lady, or a representative. ==**Determine the opposing diplomat's Courtesy with 3D6+4**== — and they may well be famous for it.
- **An opposed Courtesy contest decides who gets their desires fulfilled.**
- It may be handled with **a single Courtesy roll**, or **several across days** of negotiation.
- For particularly difficult cases the GM may impose a **reflexive −5/+5, or even −10/+10**.
- **Gifts grease the wheels** — money handed out in "gifts" is a normal part of the work.

> **Worked example (Clydno the Diplomat).** Sir Clydno negotiates with a neighbouring baron for (1) free access along the trade roads, (2) relinquishment of hunting rights in Harewood, (3) tollage rights at Highwater Bridge. His lord gives him **£10 in Roman silver**; he hands out **£4 in gifts** and makes **three opposed Diplomacy rolls** against courtiers and the baron. He **wins two** — gaining the roads and the hunting rights — but the baron **will not budge on tollage**.

## Spying at Court

To spy is to seek information from someone who wants it kept private — **a treacherous undertaking**.

- It is **hard to find time alone with anyone but the assigned escort**, who may be probed — but who ==may also have been **educated to resist Intrigue** with his own Intrigue Skill==.
- First **establish rapport** to persuade someone to talk: **Flirting**, seduction, a Skill demonstrating shared interest (**Falconry, Hunting, Heraldry, Gaming**), **giving a gift** (valued in £), **doing a Favor**, hunting or hawking together, a short adventure together, and so on.
- Then an **opposed Intrigue** resolution between the Player-knight and the informant decides the outcome — the informant **knows not to share certain things with outsiders**.

title: After the Battle — Victory, Casualties (KV) & Glory
text:
Battle ends after the maximum Battle Turns (Table 6.1 or the scenario). Major battles are usually decided by the campaign narrative; **Clash/Skirmish** outcomes are resolved by this system: **determine victory → Glory → ransom/plunder**.

## Victory or defeat (Knight Value)

A **Knight Value (KV)** = one armored, horsed knight. Tally each side's **losses** (killed or captured) in KV.

### Table 6.4 — Boy King Period Knight Values

| Troop | KV |
|-------|-----|
| Peasant | 1/16 |
| Footsoldier/Spearman/Archer | 1/8 |
| Armored Footsoldier | 1/4 |
| Hobilar/Squire/Pricker | 1/4 |
| Mounted Sergeant | 1/2 |
| Poor Knight | 3/4 |
| Knight | 1 |

If the conroi includes GM knights, the commander rolls **Table 6.5: Conroi Losses**: crit = no losses; success = 10% lost (10% captured); failure = 20% (10% killed, 10% captured); fumble = 50% (30% killed, 20% captured).

**Outcome** = (enemy KV losses ÷ friendly KV losses), then **×2** if you greatly outnumbered the foe (2:1+) or **×½** if greatly outnumbered:

- **≥4** Decisive Victory · **2–3.9** Victory · **0.5–1.9** Indecisive · **0.25–0.4** Defeat · **<0.25** Decisive Defeat.

## Glory

Every PK who fought ≥1 Encounter gets **Participation Glory** (Table 6.6), **× outcome multiplier** (Table 6.7), **× leader multiplier** (Table 6.8, if commanding a battle larger than Skirmish) — add the multipliers together before applying. This is **on top of** per-foe Encounter Glory.

### Table 6.6 — Participation Glory

| Size | Base | Tournament (rebated) |
|------|------|----------------------|
| Fight / Skirmish | 5 | 0 |
| Clash | 10 | 1 |
| Small Battle | 20 | 2 |
| Medium Battle | 30 | 3 |
| Large Battle | 45 | 5 |
| Huge Battle | 60 | 6 |

### Table 6.7 — Outcome multiplier

Decisive Victory ×2 · Victory ×1½ · Indecisive ×1 · Defeat ×¾ · Decisive Defeat ×½.

### Table 6.8 — Leader multiplier

Conroi Commander ×2 · Bataille Commander ×3 · Army Commander ×5. (E.g. a conroi commander on a Victory: ×(2+1½) = **×3½** base Glory.)

Finally, resolve **ransom and plunder** from captured foes (see [[core.wealth.ransom]]).

title: Battlefield Position, Retiring to the Rear & Surrender
text:
## Battlefield positions

**Engaged/On the Field** (choosing Encounters and fighting) · **Retire to the Rear** (the action of moving off the field) · **Out of the Battle** (behind the lines recovering) · **Left the Field** (no longer in the battle).

## Retiring to the Rear

The conroi **must** retire when Morale hits **0** or is too low for the chosen Encounter (no combat, no Glory). Otherwise the commander decides (possible Prudent/Cowardly check); if called mid-combat, each engaged PK must **Evade** or finish their fight first.

Retiring takes the conroi out for **≥1 Battle Turn** and restores **+1D6 Morale**. Attendants may treat wounds (roll a random **First Aid 14+1D6** per knight); lost horses may be replaced (Squire Skill or Horsemanship). The commander may stay disengaged, gaining **+1D6 Morale/turn** up to the starting value — then must return next turn or declare the conroi has **Left the Field**.

## Alone on the Field

Caused by deserting, Passion-Madness, or being unhorsed and failing the Squire roll for a remount. The PK becomes their own commander, rolling Battle at **−10**, and **still deducts from the conroi's Morale** (faster drain). A **maddened** knight uses a personal Morale of **1D6 + the driving Passion's value** (at 0, they vanish Out of Game). Afterward they may continue alone (mandatory if Mad), **seek their conroi** (unmodified Recognize), **rally a new conroi** (Glory Roll → Morale 2D6+3, or 2D6+6 on a crit; but Battle **−5** for the rest of the battle), or Retire to the Rear (a Valorous 16+ knight checks Cowardly unless Debilitated).

## Surrender

GM characters at **half HP or less** roll unopposed **Valorous** (−5 if on foot vs a mounted PK):

- **Critical:** fight on until dead/unconscious.
- **Success:** fight one more round, then roll again.
- **Failure:** attempt to flee.
- **Fumble:** immediate surrender.

**Fleeing:** both mounted → opposed **Horsemanship**; both on foot → opposed **DEX**; mounted fleeing a footman → escapes; footman fleeing a rider → caught unless allowed. PKs choose how long to fight; a foe caught fleeing may surrender or fight on (later surrender may require the opponent to pass a **Merciful** roll).

title: Being Charged — Countercharge, Table 6.3 Fumbles & Receiving a Charge
text:
**A Player-knight does not choose to be charged. In a Battle the enemy comes at you two ways — the *Countercharge*, when lance-armed foes ride into your charge, and the *Fumble* row of Table 6.3, which turns the charge around onto you. What you *do* control is your response, declared at the Combat Round level: `Set Spear` is the dedicated counter, and a countercharge of your own is the alternative.**

There is ==no rule for deliberately electing to receive a charge== — no brace or hold Posture that invites the enemy onto your spears at the Battle-Turn level. Being charged is handed to you by the dice; the choice happens afterwards, in Step One of the Combat Round.

## 1 · Chance of Countercharge

Opponents armed with lances — **mounted knights, mounted sergeants, Northern prickers** — **always countercharge** the Player-knights if encountered on the **first Battle Turn**.

On **subsequent turns**, roll **1D6**:

- **1–2:** Yes — they still have lances and the room to countercharge.
- **3–6:** No — their lances are shattered, or they saw the danger too late.

*GM Book, ch. 6 — Battle, p. 136.*

## 2 · Table 6.3 — Mounted Charge Opportunity

At **Step 1** of each Battle Turn the commander rolls `Battle` for a Mounted Charge Opportunity — **except on turn 1**.

| Battle roll | Engaged last round | Unengaged last round |
|-------------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| Critical | May charge | May charge (**+5 Charge**) |
| Success | May not charge | May charge |
| Failure | May not charge | May not charge |
| Fumble | **Enemy knights charge you!** | **Enemy knights charge you!** |

> [!important] Turn 1 is a mutual charge by default
> **First Charge:** unless the Army Commander failed, **turn 1 is always a mounted lance charge** — all pick Mounted Charge and only **Reckless or Valorous** Posture. Combined with the automatic countercharge above, turn 1 against feudal cavalry is a charge met by a charge, every time.

*GM Book, ch. 6 — Battle, pp. 125–131.*

## 3 · Which foes countercharge

Numbers are **per Player-knight**. Countercharging foes attack with the **Spear (Charge)** line of their statblock, not their melee spear or sword.

| Foe | Countercharges? | Charge attack |
|---|---|---|
| **Mounted Knights / Elite Mounted Knights** | **Yes** — except on a charge they prefer **swords**, unless facing long weapons | Spear (Charge) 13, **6D6** |
| **Mounted Sergeants** | **Yes** — trained in mounted tactics | Spear (Charge) 13, **5D6** |
| **Hobilars** | **No** — they automatically attempt **Evade** as the knights close | Spear 14, **3D6** |

*GM Book, ch. 6 — Battle (Feudal Foes), pp. 140–141.*

## 4 · Receiving the charge

- **It is an opposed contest, not a free hit.** A Mounted Charge resolves as **Charge vs. the opponent's Action** — whatever you declared. The charger gets **+5** if using a **couched** spear or lance against anyone *not* using a Long-reach weapon.
- **`Set Spear` is the dedicated counter.** The butt of the spear is set against or into the ground, angled at the rider or the mount. **Distance: Long. Contest: `Spear` vs. opponent's Action.** A **two-handed grip adds +2D6 damage**; a one-handed grip keeps a shield. ==It only works against an opponent using the `Charge` Skill== — against anything else it counts as a simple Attack.
- **Timing is settled by DEX.** When one character sets a spear and the other makes a Mounted Charge, resolve the conflicting declarations with **opposed DEX rolls**. Declarations are made from **lowest DEX to highest**, and the winner resolves first in Step Two.
- **Countercharging back needs room.** A charge requires at least **six yards** per charging character, so two characters charging **each other must start at least twelve yards apart**. Maximum charge distance is the horse's Movement Rate at a gallop in one Combat Round.
- **The charger still overshoots.** A Mounted Charge **must continue in a Pass-by** whether it hit or missed. On a Win or mutual miss the rider sets the distance; on a **Tie (double success), Partial Success, or Loss** the maximum is **halved and the rider must go the full distance** — so a foe who charges you ends the round past you, and a well-met countercharge leaves them badly placed.

*Core rules, ch. 7 — Combat, pp. 132–133 (declaration), 138 (distance), 140–141 (charge), 142–143 (Set Spear), 148–151 (Pass-by).*

## 5 · If your own charge goes wrong

A countercharge is resolved with the same results as any Mounted Charge, so the **Fumble** row cuts both ways — against a couched spear or lance it breaks the weapon **and** triggers a `Horsemanship` roll on **Table 7.2 (Mounted Lance Charge Fumble)**, up to **3D6** damage that **armor does not protect against**. See [[action-mounted-charge]] for the full table.

title: Debilitated in Battle — Fighting On, Aggravation, and Retiring to the Rear
text:
**A Debilitated knight can still fight a Battle, but every round is a bet against Aggravation, and Battle's own procedure gives them one honourable way out — Retire to the Rear without a Cowardly check.** Debilitated is checked the instant a knight drops below their Unconscious Characteristic, takes a Major Wound, survives a Mortal Wound, fumbles First Aid, or contracts illness/poison, and it stays checked until a successful `Chirurgery` roll **and** recovery to half Total HP (core rules, ch. 11 — Injury & Health, pp. 189–192) — neither of which happens mid-Battle Turn.

## 1 · Getting there: Major Wound and Unconscious in a Battle Turn

Fighting an Encounter is ordinary melee (see [[fighting-the-battle]]); the same wound rules apply. A single blow at or above the knight's CON is a **Major Wound** — they go unconscious immediately, check `Debilitated`, and roll once on Table 11.1: Characteristic Lost. They may attempt an **Emergency Dismount** first if mounted. Dropping to HP at or below their Unconscious Characteristic through accumulated Minor Wounds has the same effect, without the Characteristic roll (core rules, ch. 11, pp. 189–192).

An **Unconscious** knight left on the field may be taken prisoner — Capture is handled in the Squire Skill step of the Battle Turn, or by an opponent withholding their blow (see [[fighting-the-battle]]).

## 2 · Fighting on while Debilitated

Nothing in the Battle Turn procedure stops a Debilitated-but-conscious knight from choosing a Posture and fighting the next Encounter — Debilitated is a Health state, not a battlefield status. But two core-rules costs follow them into every round they stay in:

> [!important] Strenuous activity while Debilitated makes Aggravation certain
> Table 11.2 rates **fighting** as Strenuous activity. A **Healthy** knight only risks Aggravation there if carrying many small wounds or below half HP; a **Debilitated** knight's Aggravation is **certain** — one or more Hit Points lost, with no wound recorded, on top of whatever the Encounter itself does, for every round they keep fighting.

- **Table 11.2 — Activity and Aggravation**

  | Activity | Examples | Healthy | Debilitated |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | No activity | rest, eat sensibly, sleep | None (best recovery) | None (best recovery) |
  | Light | short walks, conversation, short letters | None | None unless overdone |
  | Moderate | longer walks, riding (even briefly), dancing, romance, arguing | None | Possible (GM option) |
  | Strenuous | fighting, running, climbing, significant travel | Possible if many small wounds or below half HP | **Certain** |

- **A knight who is actually Unconscious — HP at or below their Unconscious Characteristic, or the instant after a Major Wound — is normally out of the fight completely: no acting, no rolls, nothing.** *Fighting beyond debilitation* is the one exception that lets them act anyway, and it works round by round, not once for the whole Encounter:
  - **Each round they want to act, roll twice: an unopposed `Energetic` roll, and a separate roll against current HP (roll equal to or under current HP to succeed).** Both must succeed. Fail either, and that round they're out — no action, same as ordinary Unconscious.
  - **Pass both, and they act normally that round** — but it costs **1 Aggravation** (1+ HP lost, no wound recorded) regardless of how the round itself goes.
  - **Instead of acting normally, they may choose to act with slow deliberation:** a **−10 penalty to all Skills** that round, in exchange for a **reduced** Aggravation cost (the book doesn't fix a number below 1 — GM's call on the spot) (core rules, ch. 11, p. 192).
- **First Aid does not clear Debilitated** from a Major or Mortal Wound, so a squire's battlefield First Aid (Squire Skill roll, see [[fighting-the-battle]]) stops one wound bleeding but does nothing about the Aggravation risk above.

## 3 · Retiring to the Rear

Ordinary Retire to the Rear is available to the whole conroi once Morale hits 0 or falls below an Encounter's minimum (see [[battlefield-position-and-surrender]]) — a Debilitated knight retires with everyone else, no separate roll required, and Attendants may treat wounds with a random First Aid 14+1D6 per knight once out.

Debilitated has one further, narrower effect of its own: a knight left **Alone on the Field** (deserted, Passion-Mad, or unhorsed with a failed Squire remount roll) who is `Valorous` 16+ would normally have to check `Cowardly` to retire instead of fighting on — **being Debilitated waives that check.** Leaving the field while too hurt to fight is not treated as cowardice by the rules as written (GM Book, ch. 6 — Battle, pp. 131–132).

## 4 · Across a multi-day Battle

A single-day Battle ends before Deterioration matters, but a Battle that runs across several days (see [[running-a-battle]]) exposes a still-Debilitated knight to the ordinary weekly clock, scaled to the gap between sessions: without a successful `Chirurgery` roll, **Deterioration** deals 1D6 damage with no wound recorded — the only healing-side consequence that applies to a knight who is still Debilitated when the next day's fighting resumes (core rules, ch. 11, pp. 192–194; see [[aggravation-and-deterioration]]). Natural Healing Rate resumes only once Chirurgery has actually restored the knight to half Total HP and cleared Debilitated (core rules, ch. 11, pp. 189–192, 198–199; see [[healing-recovery]]).

*Core rules, ch. 11 — Injury & Health, pp. 189–194, 198–199. GM Book, ch. 6 — Battle, pp. 125–132.*

title: Fighting the Battle — Turn Procedure, Postures & Encounters
text:
## Disobeying orders

Refusing a conroi leader's orders loses **1 Station and 1 Homage** (plus possible Proud/Reckless/Cowardly checks and a Suspicious/Hate from the leader), and renders the PK **Alone on the Field** (deserters don't form their own conroi).

## Battle Turn procedure

1. **Set Encounter** (GM's default). Battle **Events** keyed to the turn apply to PKs on the field. The commander rolls Battle for a **Mounted Charge Opportunity** (Table 6.3), except turn 1.
2. **Intensity roll** (GM, unopposed vs Intensity): success = Encounter stands (**crit doubles foes**, **fumble = an Opportunity**); failure = PKs may reroll.
3. **Battle roll** (each PK, if they want to change): success = choose an Encounter; **critical = choose an Opportunity**.
4. **Select Encounter** (commander); if below Minimum Morale → **Retire to the Rear**.
5. **Reduce Morale** by the Encounter's amount.
6. **Select Posture** & invoke Passions.
7. **Fight the Encounter** (rounds per Posture).
8. **Squire Skill roll** (optional).

### Table 6.3 — Mounted Charge Opportunity

| Battle roll | Engaged last round | Unengaged last round |
|-------------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| Critical | May charge | May charge (**+5 Charge**) |
| Success | May not charge | May charge |
| Failure | May not charge | May not charge |
| Fumble | Enemy knights charge you! | Enemy knights charge you! |

**First Charge:** unless the Army Commander failed, **turn 1 is always a mounted lance charge** — all pick Mounted Charge and only Reckless or Valorous Posture.

## Postures (rounds fought + Morale effect)

- **Reckless** — 3 rounds; check Reckless; **+1D3 Morale**; must Reckless-Attack round 1 (unless charging).
- **Valorous** — 2 rounds; check Valorous.
- **Prudent** — 1 round; check Prudent; **−1D3 Morale**.
- **Cowardly** — don't engage; immediately Retire to the Rear; **−1 Honor** and **−1D6 Morale** if above half HP.

## Fighting the Encounter

Normal melee; charging knights take Mounted Charge as their first Action. You may not aid an ally without a successful **Evade** first. Fight your Posture's rounds (min 1); if you drop your foe early, take a fresh one. Defeating all available foes ends the turn; a PK still engaged at turn's end may fight one more round on a successful **Energetic + Valorous**. **Passions** may be used once per battle (effect lasts one Battle Turn). After the Encounter, gain each defeated foe's **Glory**, and raise Morale by the total **KV** of foes defeated.

**Missile foes:** the commander rolls Battle to see rounds of barrage endured before contact — **crit immediate / success 1 / failure 2 / fumble 3**. Each round, 1D6: **1–4 hits the mount, 5–6 the rider**. Shields impose their Missile Penalty (no Zigzag in a conroi).

**Squire Skill roll** (unopposed, optional): success = squire helps (replace a lance ×2, give a horse, escort a prisoner, bear off an unconscious knight); **fumble = squire missing until the battle ends**. **Capture:** a knight may take an Unconscious foe prisoner (or use Brawling / withheld blows); exposing a surrendered captive to danger = **−1 Honor**.

title: Battle Foe Encounters — Foot Troops (Peasants to Elite Knights on Foot)
text:
Each Foe Encounter lists **Morale Loss** (subtracted from the conroi's Morale when taken), **Morale Minimum** (the conroi may not engage below it), and **Knight Value** for the post-battle KV tally. Numbers given are **per Player-knight**.

## Peasants — Morale Loss 1D3 · Minimum 5 · KV 1/16

Levied farmers with agricultural implements. ==No Glory in fighting them, only bloodshed.==

- **Five peasants per Player-knight.**
- **If charged by knights:** roll **Cowardly** — on a *success* they flee and are cut down by the horsemen.
- Even if they stand, **only half attack per round** (three per knight), imposing the usual Multiple Opponents penalty. A peasant **automatically flees** at the end of any round in which he takes damage.
- At the end of each round, one **collective Valorous** roll per group: **failure** = half the group flees (plus the wounded); **fumble** = the whole group flees.

| SIZ | DEX | STR | CON | | HP | Knockdown | Major Wound | Unconscious |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 10 | 10 | 8 | | 18 | 10 | 8 | 5 |

**Attack:** Agricultural Implement 8, **2D6+3** · **Movement** 15 · **AP** 0 · **Glory** 0 · **Traits:** `Valorous 6` · **Armor:** none · **Ransom:** none

## Spearmen — Morale Loss 1D6 · Minimum 8 · KV 1/8

The lowest of the proper fighting men. In a hedge of spear points they are dangerous to knights *and* horses.

- **Three spearmen per knight.** They gang up, imposing the Multiple Opponents penalty.
- **Set Spear** against a Mounted Charge requires a **Valorous** roll — ==**every** spearman in the group must succeed== for the group to use it.
- They always wield spears **two-handed** (the damage already includes the +2D6), and therefore **do not suffer the −5 height penalty** against mounted opponents.
- **Defend** (backing away slowly) once more than **one-third** are seriously injured or killed; **flee at two-thirds**.

| SIZ | DEX | STR | CON | | HP | Knockdown | Major Wound | Unconscious |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 10 | 12 | 13 | | 23 | 10 | 13 | 6 |

**Attacks:** Dagger (Brawling) 10, **2D6+4** · Spear (2H) 10, **4D6+2D6** · **Movement** 16 · **AP** 5 · **Glory** 10 · **Traits:** `Valorous 12` · **Armor:** gambeson and kettle helm · **Ransom:** none

## Foot Soldiers — Morale Loss 1D6 · Minimum 7 · KV 1/8

Mercenaries or feudal garrison in light armor with shields — tougher than peasants, but reluctant to face a lance charge.

- **Two foot soldiers per knight.** One roll sets their collective armament.
- **If charged by mounted knights:** a single **collective Valorous** roll — *any success* and all stand; **failure** = half flee; **fumble** = all flee. They also all flee once **half** their number are seriously injured or killed.
- Apply the **Height modifier** when they fight mounted knights, and the long-weapon bonus for knights with spears or lances.

| SIZ | DEX | STR | CON | | HP | Knockdown | Major Wound | Unconscious |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 10 | 12 | 13 | | 23 | 10 | 13 | 6 |

**Attacks (all Skill 10):** Battle Axe (Hafted) **4D6**\* · Mace (Hafted) **4D6**\*\* · Sword **4D6** — \* −1D6 Shield Protection, \*\* +1D6 vs mail · **Movement** 16 · **AP** 5+6 · **Glory** 10 · **Armor:** light armor + shield · **Ransom:** none

## Archers — Morale Loss 1D6 · Minimum 5 · KV 1/8

*"Cowardly scum, shooting at good knights!"*

- **Three archers per Player-knight.** One roll sets their collective armament.
- They **loose as soon as the knights enter long range** — use **Closing Distance** (Core Rulebook p. 152) for how many rounds they get, assuming a **canter** if the knights are charging, otherwise a **trot**. Against mounted knights roll **1D6: 1–4 hits the horse, 5–6 the rider**.
- If the conroi reaching them has **more mounted than dismounted knights**, each archer must make a **Valorous** roll or flee. The whole unit flees once **one-third** are seriously injured or killed.

| SIZ | DEX | STR | CON | | HP | Knockdown | Major Wound | Unconscious |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 9 | 10 | 15 | 15 | | 24 | 9 | 15 | 6 |

**Attacks:** Light Crossbow 12, **1D6+10** · Self Bow 12, **3D6** · Dagger (Brawling) 10, **2D6+4** · **Movement** 18 · **AP** 1 or 5 · **Glory** 5 · **Traits:** `Valorous 8`

## Knights on Foot — Morale Loss 1D6 · Minimum 10 · KV 1/2
## Elite Knights on Foot — Morale Loss 1D6+2 · Minimum 12 · KV 1/2

Dismounted by mishap or by choice, and every bit as deadly. The Elite are a lord's bodyguard in fine harness. **Both use the same statblock.**

- **1½ times as many as there are Player-knights** (round up).
- They **double up** on the Player-knights where possible, targeting those with **the most Glory and the best-looking equipment and horses** first; the rest fight one-on-one.
- Their **spears negate the −5 height penalty** against a mounted opponent. Against foes on foot they prefer **swords**.
- Roll ransom **individually** for each knight captured.

| SIZ | DEX | STR | CON | | HP | Knockdown | Major Wound | Unconscious |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 14 | 11 | 12 | 14 | | 28 | 14 | 14 | 7 |

**Attacks:** Spear 12, **4D6**\* (\*negates height penalty) · Sword 15, **4D6** · **Movement** 17 · **AP** 10+6 · **Glory** 25 · **Traits:** `Valorous 15` · **Armor:** hauberk, aketon, and nasal helm + kite shield

**Ransom (1D6):** 1 Poor Knight **£3** · 2–5 Household Knight **£4** · 6 Vassal Knight **£10**

title: Battle Foe Encounters — Mounted Troops (Hobilars, Sergeants, Knights)
text:
Numbers are **per Player-knight**. Lance-armed foes may countercharge — see [[gm.battle.plunder-and-encounters]].

> **Note a discrepancy:** the Knight Values printed in these Foe Encounters (Hobilar **1/2**, Mounted Sergeant **3/4**) differ from **Table 6.4** in *After the Battle*, which gives Hobilar/Squire/Pricker **1/4** and Mounted Sergeant **1/2**. Pick one and use it consistently for the whole KV tally.

## Hobilars — Morale Loss 1D6+3 · Minimum 10 · KV 1/2 (cf. Table 6.4: 1/4)

Lightly-armed scouts and pursuers on swift "hobby" horses. They want no part of a conroi of knights, and offer **little Glory and no ransom**.

- **Two hobilars per Player-knight.**
- As the knights close, they **automatically attempt Evade**; their hobby horses' **Movement Rate is 18**. A knight chasing both counts as **fighting multiple opponents (−5 per action)**; concentrate on one and ==the other automatically flees.==
- If caught, a hobilar fights **at least one Combat Round**, then tests **Valorous** — failure means another Evade attempt next round, success means another round of combat.

| SIZ | DEX | STR | CON | | HP | Knockdown | Major Wound | Unconscious |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 15 | 10 | 13 | | 23 | 10 | 13 | 6 |

**Attack:** Spear 14, **3D6** · **Movement** 18 · **AP** 6+6 · **Glory** 25 · **Skills & Traits:** `Horsemanship 16`, `Valorous 10` · **Armor:** gambeson and nasal helm + kite shield · **Ransom:** none

## Mounted Sergeants — Morale Loss 1D6+2 · Minimum 12 · KV 3/4 (cf. Table 6.4: 1/2)

Non-noble warriors trained to fight from horseback. Also use this block for **esquires, poor mercenary knights without squires**, and other better-off cavalry.

- **As many sergeants as there are Player-knights.**
- They ride **small chargers**, armed and equipped like knights but not as well.
- Trained in mounted tactics, so they **may countercharge**.
- Usually **not worth a ransom** — but determine it individually, since some are esquires or poor mercenary knights.

| SIZ | DEX | STR | CON | | HP | Knockdown | Major Wound | Unconscious |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 13 | 10 | 12 | 15 | | 28 | 13 | 15 | 7 |

**Attacks:** Spear (Charge) 13, **5D6** · Spear 7, **4D6** · Sword 13, **4D6** · **Movement** 15 · **AP** 9+6 · **Glory** 25 · **Skills & Traits:** `Horsemanship 14`, `Valorous 12` · **Armor:** hauberk, aketon, and open helm + kite shield · **Ransom (1D6):** 5–6 Poor Mercenary **£2**

## Mounted Knights — Morale Loss 1D6+2 · Minimum 12 · KV 1
## Elite Mounted Knights — Morale Loss 2D6 · Minimum 12 · KV 1

**Both use the same statblock.** The Elite ride **fine stallions worth £5 more** than normal chargers, and their captured horses may have received training.

- **As many as there are Player-knights.**
- They **may countercharge**. Except on a charge they prefer **swords**, unless facing long weapons.

| SIZ | DEX | STR | CON | | HP | Knockdown | Major Wound | Unconscious |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 14 | 11 | 12 | 14 | | 28 | 14 | 14 | 7 |

**Attacks:** Spear (Charge) 13, **6D6** · Spear 12, **4D6** · Sword 15, **4D6** · **Movement** 16 · **AP** 10+6 · **Glory** 25 · **Skills & Traits:** `Horsemanship 15`, `Valorous 15` · **Armor:** hauberk, aketon, and nasal helm + kite shield
